In the third release, area-wide growth was upgraded to 0.6%qoq due to the Irish revision, while ex-Ireland growth was essentially unchanged at +0.3% as revisions in Germany (+0.10pp to +0.33%) and France (-0.12pp to +0.04%) broadly offset each other. Real GDP growth was supported by firm consumption growth, which more than offset a modest drag from declining real investment, and resilient foreign demand (Exhibit 1, left). The data received so far for Q3, however, has been more mixed. Soft data has continued to recover in the first two months of Q3 and, on net, stands close to pre-conflict levels. Across sectors, manufacturing survey data has been particularly encouraging in Q3 and retail indicators have also risen. Survey indicators of spot activity in the services sectors have lagged slightly behind but have nonetheless unwound most of the weakness observed in Q2 (Exhibit 1, right). The BSP already increased its policy rate 50bp this year thru July. We believe the BSP may raise its policy rate 25bp more in Aug-2026, which may be the last hike in this tightening cycle, leaving the policy rate at 5.0%. Singapore Growth: We revise up our 2026 GDP growth forecast by 60bps to 5.1%, with near-term growth bolstered by broad-based domestic electronics upcycle (across semis, disk media and PCs). Meanwhile, labour market conditions remain healthy, and should keep domestic demand expanding at around trend-pace. Inflation: We expect core inflation to hover around 2-2.3% - and above the historical average of 1.5-2% - at least through mid-2027. Factors that would push core inflation higher include imported cost pressures and F&B services (after mandatory wage increases kicked in from 1st Jul). Policy: We tentatively see MAS steepening the slope “very slightly” by 25bps in Oct, based on the view that MAS sees a greater risk of core inflation not moderating discernibly around mid-2027. In any case, the bar for a 25bps “very slight” steepening is lower than for a “slight” move, which both we and market participants generally interpret as a 50bps slope increase. The CDU suffered heavy losses, falling to 17.2% and 16 seats, while the SPD (9.3%, 8 seats), Greens (8.9%, 7 seats), and Left Party (8.6%, 8 seats) all entered parliament. The BSW, a far-left outfit with ideological overlaps with the AfD on matters such as a more Russia-friendly foreign policy, also cleared the 5% threshold and won 5 seats. records.text: earch We stay Positive on Large-over-Small for the following reasons: • The increased prospect of a new Fed tightening cycle creates a less favorable backdrop for smaller companies. Historically, small caps have struggled relative to large caps once rate hikes begin, and the current environment appears particularly challenging given that 32% of small-cap companies remain unprofitable and leverage has risen to 3.5x net debt/EBITDA, near post-COVID highs. In addition, earnings revisions have lagged those of large caps, suggesting weaker fundamental momentum heading into a more restrictive policy regime. • Relative valuation and positioning dynamics also favor large caps. Small-cap valuations have steadily expanded despite deteriorating earnings revisions, while Big Tech and other mega- cap leaders have undergone a meaningful de-rating. This combination leaves small caps with less margin for error and creates greater scope for valuation compression should rates move higher. Taken together, weaker balance sheets, softer earnings trends, and a less attractive valuation backdrop underpin our continued Positive stance on the Large-over-Small Size factor. 8 September 2026 11 Barclays | U.S. Equity Factor Insights - September 2026

Under these arrangements, the private partner finances, builds and owns the infrastructure and leases it to the p ublic sector. The public sector uses and operates the facility and pays rent to the private partner. Maintenance may be undertaken by either the private or the public partner. Such arrangements may be suitable for administrative buildings, for example. Man agement contracts represent a further form of PPP. Under these contracts, private companies assume responsibility for managing and operating a public facility or service in return for a fee. However, they do not invest extensively in the infrastructure or assume the financing risks. Ownership and responsibility for investment remain with the state. In a broader sense, municipal utilities (Stadtwerke) can also be regarded as a form of public -private partnership. Municipal utilities are typically at least partly owned by a municipality, such as a city or a larger local authority, or are otherwise under municipal influence. They often have a public -service mandate covering areas such as water, wastewater, energy and local public transport. The municipality exercises an ownership and/or supervisory function to ensure that the public-service mandate is fulfilled. Both long only and hedge fund managers were net buyers last week. Long-only increased exposure in most sectors, especially Tech and Financials. Hedge funds bought back some Tech and added Industrials. Top three sectors based on the last 2m of flows were Health Care, Real Estate, and Materials, while Consumer Staples, Financials, and Tech were the bottom three. Our market-implied regime analysis suggests that market internals are currently most correlated with the "Tightening financial conditions" regimes as earlier hopes of "Goldilocks"/"Recovery" have materially faded. Continued geopolitical risks have provided a tailwind to Energy, while a hawkish speech from Chair Warsh at Jackson Hole and a strong US employment report prompted markets to reprice rates higher, causing headwind to rates sensitive sectors like Utilities, Real Estate, and Tech. Taken together, the resulting sector rotation strengthened expectations of "Tighter financial conditions". We expect it to look through also the latest spike in gas prices and rising bond yields. We see GDP growth being close to 1% this year and accelerating to 1.5% in 2027. Stockpile and invest — We argue that the Eurozone economy keeps (slowly) growing not despite the exogenous shocks, but precisely because of them. Relentless challenges—from surging energy prices to trade tensions—have rendered capital expenditure and building inventory buffers a necessity. Higher gas prices are unlikely to be a major threat, in our view, given the notable downsizing that has already occurred to energy-intensive sectors since 2022. records.text: Our Detailed Q3 Tracking Estimate With the still-limited data available, we refine our area-wide Q3 tracking estimate and launch our country-level nowcasts. In Germany, our tracking has moderated significantly following the sharp -3.4%mom decline in real retail sales reported for July. A -16.1% drop in real sales at chemists— likely driven by a regulatory change in the reimbursement rules under the statutory health insurance—weighed on the print but spending on several other items was also weak. While German retail sales have been subject to large upwards revisions over the last few months, for now we see the print as pointing to a slight contraction in real consumption in Q3. Furthermore, the moderation in real manufacturing sales and industrial production in July—which reflects car plant retooling and, possibly, a drag from low Rhine levels and the fading impulse from strategic stock-building in some energy-intensive sectors—is weighing on our nowcast of industrial GVA in Q3. records.text: ment would be complete without considering another factor, even if it lies beyond the primary scope of this report: supply-side constraints. Even with significantly improved regulatory frameworks and faster approval pr ocedures, infrastructure investment cannot be expanded indefinitely and at will. Actual implementation is likely to encounter capacity constraints over the coming years. Shortages already exist among engineers, planners, site managers and skilled construction workers. These challenges are compounded by limited capacity at construction and infrastructure companies, long lead times for certain intermediate inputs, and heavy workloads among specialized planning and permitting authorities. The demographic decline in the labor force is likely to exacerbate these challenges further in the years ahead. As a result, the pace at which infrastructure projects can be delivered will depend not only on financing and regulation, but also on the availability of sufficient human, material and organizational resources. Despite these constraints, attractive investment opportunities are likely to emerge in the German infrastructure market for both institutional and strategic investors. Whether infrastructure investment and private capital ultimately prove to be a “perfect match”, however, will depend heavily on the specific infrastructure sector under consideration. Electricity generation, energy trading and energy supply operate in Germany within a liberalized environment. The state defines the regulatory framework, which is monitored by institutions such as the Federal Cartel Office and the Federal Network Agency. The government also sets expansion targets for renewable energy installations and gas-fired power plants, influences end-user electricity and gas prices through taxes and levies, and pursues the goal of climate neutrality, which directly affects the energy sector. Source: Barclays Research Baseline expectations Turning to the different channels by which aggregate inflation could be pushed higher by the secular growth in energy and electricity demand, the natural first path is via modal/baseline expectations. In essence, excess energy demand should translate into sustained upward pressure on energy commodities (for more details on this, please see the Commodities in Focus section of the recent cross-asset report). This is an essential factor for assessing inflation risk, as many economists/investors rely on commodity futures curves to project market-implied forward raw commodity prices and, by extension, inflation. If our thesis is correct, and the supply/demand imbalance leads to sustained upward pressure on prices of raw materials, this should translate into higher commodities futures prices and, thus, higher baseline inflation forecasts. In addition, it is not only the level of the curve, but also the shape that informs inflation risk. For instance, if the entire commodity curve shifts higher, but the curve does not steepen, then in essence the price action implies a one-off price-level shock, rather than a sustained inflation process

Source: Barclays Research Baseline expectations Turning to the different channels by which aggregate inflation could be pushed higher by the secular growth in energy and electricity demand, the natural first path is via modal/baseline expectations. In essence, excess energy demand should translate into sustained upward pressure on energy commodities (for more details on this, please see the Commodities in Focus section of the recent cross-asset report). This is an essential factor for assessing inflation risk, as many economists/investors rely on commodity futures curves to project market-implied forward raw commodity prices and, by extension, inflation. If our thesis is correct, and the supply/demand imbalance leads to sustained upward pressure on prices of raw materials, this should translate into higher commodities futures prices and, thus, higher baseline inflation forecasts. In addition, it is not only the level of the curve, but also the shape that informs inflation risk. For instance, if the entire commodity curve shifts higher, but the curve does not steepen, then in essence the price action implies a one-off price-level shock, rather than a sustained inflation process

records.text: Low Global and SPR Oil Stocks Don’t Imply Crude Prices Have to Jump Imminently Visible global oil stocks (Exhibit 10, left) and OECD SPR levels (Exhibit 9) are low by historical standards. Even so, they do not necessarily imply a crude price spike if Middle East supply continues to recover, for three reasons: history, our view that we aren’t running out of oil in the near-term, and China’s price-sensitive imports. Reason 1: History The historical relationship between prices and global visible oil stocks is weak. In fact, when visible global stocks hit their all time low in November 2024 (in a sample starting in February 2017), Brent was $76 (Exhibit 10, left).1 The latest OECD commercial stocks measured in days of demand—which predict oil prices better than global stocks— remain 16% above their 2003 average all-time low. In 2003, Brent front-to-back 1M/36M timespreads traded around a relatively high but not extreme 20% (and Brent spot prices around $30 (Exhibit 10, right)).2 1 To be clear, late 2024 was a different environment from today with high OPEC spare capacity and limited supply disruptions. 2 OECD commercial landed stocks were structurally lower before the US shale boom. The structural increase in OECD commercial stocks can be explained by a shift from storage on water (given long-haul voyages from the Middle East) to landed crude storage in the US (and short-haul voyages). Electricity networks benefit from regulated network charges that generate relatively predictable cash flows. Recent investments by international pension funds and sovereign wealth funds in parts of the German transmission network demonstrate that institutional investors are prepared to provide equity capital for German energy infrastructure. Hydrogen projects are more difficult to assess. Although investment requirements are substantial along the entire value chain, commercial viability remains highly dependent on support programs, regulatory conditions and the development of sufficient demand . For the time being, hydrogen is therefore more likely to be an investment field for strategic investors with operational expertise than for conservative infrastructure investors. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 08 September 2026 49 Peru: Revising down growth because of El Niño Meteorological agencies across the world expect “global” (ENSO, central Pacific, zones 3-4) and “coastal” (eastern Pacific, zones 1-2) El Niños to materialize strongly and simultaneously, between 4Q2026 and 1Q2027, for the first time since 1982-1983 and 1997-1998. Though this distinction (“global” vs. “coastal”) is irrelevant in most countries, Peruvian policymakers pay close attention to it because of the different economic effects. The “global” El Niño is associated with warmer weather & ocean temperatures, and droughts in the highlands/Andes, lowering fishing and agricultural supply. Whereas the “coastal” El Niño typically comes with severe floodings along the coast, impacting fishing and agriculture, but also transportation, manufacturing, commerce, and mining. Arguably, the coastal El Niño is a worse shock. Against this backdrop, we are lowering our GDP growth forecast for 2027, to 4% from 4.4%. Nevertheless, this number is still significantly above-consensus (3.1%, based on eighteen firms surveyed by Bloomberg) and implies an acceleration compared to 2026 (which we forecast at 3.5%). In our view, the positive terms of trade shock (driven by metal prices) coupled with the soaring business confidence (to ~10-year highs after the new government assumed office) will more than offset El Niño’s temporary drag. Gradual appreciation path to continue We continue to expect further gradual CNY appreciation in the months ahead as discussed in detail in China - CNY appreciation delayed, not derailed. First, we maintain our view that Chinese's authorities are comfortable with a gradual appreciation trend. Last week, the PBoC set the USD/CNY fixing at its strongest level since February 2023, while at the same time allowing the gap between the official fixing and the market-expected fixing to widen to its largest since earlier this year. In our view, this is consistent with a preference for a firmer currency, albeit at a controlled pace. Second, we think the PBoC is paying close attention to the CFETS CNY trade-weighted index, which has remained broadly stable in a 102-103 range since mid-June. USD weakness has given the authorities greater scope to guide the CNY stronger against the USD without triggering a sharp appreciation in the trade-weighted basket. We expect this pattern to persist ahead of the Xi-Trump summit, leaving the CNY biased towards further modest appreciation in the period surrounding the meeting. A long -term criterion applies to 9 GW of the planned capacity, meaning that these installations must be capable of providing electricity continuously for extended periods. While this requirement does not apply exclusively to gas-fired power plants, modern and highly efficient gas-fired facilities represent the most typical solution. These plants must also be capable of conversion to hydrogen operation (H2-ready) in order to enable climate - neutral operation from 2045 onwards. From an investor’s perspective, an important aspect is that the construction of these facilities is expected to be supported financially. Beginning in 2031, funding is to be provided through a new levy on electricity consumers. This means that backup capacity will not have to be refinanced solely through electricity sales. Instead, operators will receive payments for providing secured capacity. As the average annual utilization rates of these new facilities are likely to remain low, and could decline further as renewable energy and storage capacity continue expanding, a business model based solely on electricity sales during periods of low renewable generation or peak demand would involve considerable uncertainty. Although the details of the future support regime have not yet been finalized, it appears likely that the desired investments are more likely to materialize within a capacity market than under a pure energy -on

We now focus on exposures to services provided by these industries. For this part, the data available only allow us to separate by income cohort, but we can infer results about the other demographic groups. If disinflation first occurs in these categories of spending, high-income cohorts could experience lower inflation rates relative to the aggregate. Additional upside risks stem from tax reform, which is likely to increase the relative taxation of services, the IPCA basket rebasing based on the new POF, and discussions surrounding changes to the 6x1 work schedule. Nevertheless, we expect inflation to moderate to 4.7% by YE27 and 3.5% by YE28 as a smaller fiscal and credit impulse, combined with the lagged effects of restrictive monetary policy, leading to weaker demand and greater economic slack. Monetary: no pause in the easing cycle We are revising our Selic forecasts and no longer expect the BCB to pause its easing cycle. Our new baseline scenario envisages the policy rate ending 2026 at 13.25% (previously 13.75%), 2027 at 11.25% (previously 12.75%), and 2028 at 11.25% (previously 11.75%). records.text: Bank Rate's position as the active tool in the July MPR box suggests to us that the same logic still holds. With Bank Rate significantly above the effective lower bound, there is no sense that the MPC is restricted in its ability to set Bank Rate more loosely if it feels tightening gilt yields are inconsistent with its monetary policy objective. QT has a fiscal cost when fiscal policy is tight. Slowing unwind would help public finances. It is true that unwinding the gilt portfolio crystallises losses and requires fiscal transfers. Under the assumption that Bank Rate stays at 3.75% and the BoE unwinds by £50bn, we estimate this cost would be around £17bn between October 2026 and September 2027 (Figure 9). However, over half of this would be interest losses (negative carry) on the gilt portfolio, which would actually be exacerbated by a slower unwind. Just over £6bn comes from losses inflicted by sales. Were the MPC to choose to halt active sales, this would remove that £6bn loss but increase interest losses, meaning the saving would be closer to £5bn, The slower unwind would also increase interest losses in future years due to the larger portfolio. Adjusting QT in response to fiscal considerations also risks appearing to allow fiscal influence over MPC's decisions on how to achieve its remit, which Chief Economist Pill warned about recently and was one of the reasons the indemnity on the APF was enacted in the first place. Weekly data through 28 Aug 2026. We construct four components: 1) risk reversals, 2) MSCI France/MSCI Europe ratio, 3) 10y OAT-Bund spreads, and 4) FX positioning. In the first step of the process, we construct the components for risk reversals and FX positioning. For risk reversals we use an equally weighted average of the full-sample z-scores applied to EUR-USD and EUR-CHF risk reversals, 3 months and 1 year ahead. For FX positioning we use a simple average of the z-scores for the CFTC data (non-commercials, TFF Asset Managers, and TFF Leveraged Funds) and SDR FX options. In the second step of the process, we generate full- sample z-scores for all four components separately (re-standardising onto a common scale) and then take their simple average. In the third step of the process, we calculate the full-sample z- score of that average, which becomes our proxy for France-related risks. Throughout, the signs of individual components have been adjusted so that higher z-scores suggest higher France-related concerns. Our approach is inspired by Lina Fransson and Oskar Tysklind (2017), An index for financial conditions in Sweden, Sveriges Riksbank Economic Review 2017:1. records.text: With this in mind, the past decades of 'hyperglobalisation' may have been the exception rather than the norm. In a global economy that had become increasingly integrated, the trade of primary energy sources such as oil, coal and gas was driven largely by efficiency considerations – just like all other supply chains. There was a clear pattern between exporters (the Middle East, Russia, Norway, Canada, Nigeria and other EM economies) and importers (the US, Europe, Japan, China, and India). Rising geopolitical fragmentation and technological advances have started to change this over the past decade or so. Russia’s war with Ukraine suddenly upended the important flow of Russian pipeline gas to Europe, forcing it to look for alternatives such as LNG shipments from other regions. Similarly, the ongoing disruption of the flow of oil and gas through the Strait of Hormuz has now also made the Gulf region a less reliable source of energy imports, including LNG. Regarding technologically driven change, the shale gas/tight oil revolution in the US stands out. It has turned the US from the world's largest oil importer into a net exporter. In contrast, Germany’s decision to fully exit its nuclear technology at home has made Europe’s largest economy more reliant on energy imports. More recently, China's mass production of low-cost green technologies is helping to boost electricity generation from renewable sources such as sunlight and wind across the globe. For starters, the heatwaves became even more intense over the summer months, potentially dampening agricultural activity further – a shock that will never be captured by business surveys, focused on manufacturing and services. Gas prices have increased, with a potentially more adverse effect on production than oil. Besides, the indirect effect of higher energy prices should soon start to feed through to inflation, while tighter financing and credit conditions weigh on already -weak investment, especially residential. France and Europe are also benefiting relatively less from the immediate demand impulse associated with the global AI investment boom than the world average, as we discussed here. In this case, the value of the semiconductors would be captured once when they are initially imported and again as part of the value of the servers when they return to the US. Not accounting for re-exports means we are netting out too many imports when assessing the contribution of AI to GDP. To account for re-exports, we estimate the share of imports that remain in the US using Census Bureau data on imports and re-exports over an annual window. Because goods may be imported and re-exported multiple times, using an annual window reduces short- term noise and provides a more reliable estimate of the share of imports that ultimately remains in the United States. Our estimates indicate that re-exports account for a meaningful share of imports of both computers and peripherals and semiconductors and related devices, as shown in Exhibit 3 . In 2025, we estimate that only about 86% of imported computers and peripherals remained in the United States, while the corresponding share for semiconductors and related devices was approximately 53%. The ongoing US-Iran war and its consequences for shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and in part also the Bab-el-Mandeb Strait has reignited the discussion around 'choke points'; ie, narrow maritime corridors through which a large share of the world’s oil, gas, grains and manufactured goods must pass. Next to the two straits mentioned, the Strait of Malacca, the Suez Canal, Panama Canal and the Turkish Straits (Bosporus, Dardanelles) are typically mentioned. However, the true geo-economic significance requires closer inspection. Although interruptions of flows through such shipping bottlenecks do affect the global trading system, the recent experience has been that the eventual economic impact has often been less severe than initially thought: eg, Germany avoided the worst-case-scenario of having to shut down its industries when Russia gas was cut off in 2022-23, the disruption of Ukrainian grain exports due to Russia's attack never led to the extreme global shortages some had feared, and even the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz – considered by experts a supply disruption much worse than that of the 1970s oil crises2 – has not (yet) been proportionally impactful on the oil price. records.text: 8 September 2026 Focus Germany Deutsche Bank AG Page 2 1. Introduction: Special fund to strengthen infrastructure Infrastructure forms the backbone of an economy. In many infrastructure segments, utilization has increased in recent years, for example due to rising transport volumes and growing data traffic. Other areas are characterized by a structural shift in public policy, most notably the energy transition. As a result of these developments, the demands placed on the resilience and performance of Germany’s infrastructure have increased. At the same time, insufficient investment has meant that many infrastructure assets are no longer fully capable of meeting these higher requirements and are in a state of disrepair in numerous areas. This is weighing on the country’s economic and social development. Against this backdrop, the Federal G overnment has set itself the objective of strengthening public infrastructure over the coming years. In March 2025, the German Bundestag approved the Special Fund for Infrastructure and Climate Neutrality ( SVIK). The fund represents a borrowing authorization that enables the federal government to undertake an additional EUR 500 bn of public investment over a period of twelve years, on top of the investments financed through the federal core budget. In logic applications, there are three to four firing processes within the packaging flow, and the optimal carrier is selected for each process. As a result, both glass and ceramic carriers are used. In HBM applications, support glass is used during the grinding process. Carrier flatness of less than 1μm is required, and glass offers superior flatness compared with ceramics. Consequently, only glass carriers are used in HBM applications. The company's current market share in semiconductor SG, including both glass and ceramic carriers and across both logic and memory applications, is approximately 50%. records.text: g wage growth remains solid On a continuously surveyed firm basis, which excludes the impact of sample changes, total cash earnings per worker slowed from 4.8% yoy in June to 2.8% in July, below the 4.2% market consensus. The main driver was a slowdown in special cash earnings to 2.7% from 7.1% in June. Base pay for full-time workers, a key gauge of underlying wage trends, also edged down to 2.7% from 2.9%. Since January 2026, there has been a substantial divergence between the full-sample headline series and the continuously surveyed firm series, both in scheduled cash earnings growth and special cash earnings, complicating the assessment of wage trends. records.text: 6 Liquid Insight | 08 September 2026 Exhibit 12: France-related risks seem partly priced… A vanilla proxy for France-related risks (higher values = higher risks) Source: BofA Global Research, Bloomberg. Weekly data through 28 Aug 2026. We construct four components: 1) risk reversals, 2) MSCI France/MSCI Europe ratio, 3) 10y OAT-Bund spreads, and 4) FX positioning. In the first step of the process, we construct the components for risk reversals and FX positioning. For risk reversals we use an equally weighted average of the full-sample z-scores applied to EUR-USD and EUR-CHF risk reversals, 3 months and 1 year ahead. For FX positioning we use a simple average of the z-scores for the CFTC data (non-commercials, TFF Asset Managers, and TFF Leveraged Funds) and SDR FX options. In the second step of the process, we generate full- sample z-scores for all four components separately (re-standardising onto a common scale) and then take their simple average. In the third step of the process, we calculate the full-sample z- score of that average, which becomes our proxy for France-related risks. Throughout, the signs of individual components have been adjusted so that higher z-scores suggest higher France-related concerns. Our approach is inspired by Lina Fransson and Oskar Tysklind (2017), An index for financial conditions in Sweden, Sveriges Riksbank Economic Review 2017:1. Again, in late-2015 into early-2016, heightened recession fears (just as the Fed began to hike rates again) also drove an equity selloff alongside wider credit spreads. n In recent years, this has often been staved off by some sort of monetary or fiscal stimulus, which in turn has supported risk assets. But that is much more difficult in the current context: n First, because headline and core inflation are already above target in many countries, easing monetary policy is not an easily available option like we saw in the 2010s. So something like the Fed’s easing in 2019 (which occurred in the context of below-target inflation) is much more difficult to imagine. n Second, fiscal stimulus is also more difficult today, because bond yields are around multi-year highs and the debt-to-GDP ratios have risen significantly. So a meaningful fiscal stimulus is not an easily available option either. In other words, policymakers don’t have easily available tools to support risk assets if they do come under pressure. records.text: and, to a lesser extent, household equipment recorded above -average rises (Figure 2). Firmer apparel prices are not new in our data, but goods inflation appears to be quietly strengthening again. Our more granular L3 data reinforce that signal: the central forecast for core CPI (seasonally adjusted) is 0.28%, the highest since the start of the year and, for the first time since February, above consensus (Figure 3). Partly, this reflects a long-awaited consensus adjustment. Forecasts had been anchored near 0.3% for most of the past 18 months; after eleven downside surprises, eight captured by PriceStats, they have finally shifted lower. As Figure 4 shows, an unusually large share of forecasts now sits at 0.2%, with few assigning risk to a firmer print. Our estimate is only four basis points above consensus, before rounding, but it suggests that confidence may be misplaced. A single 0.3% rise in core CPI would not be especially troubling; annual core CPI would remain at 2.5%. But the PPI and CPI components feeding into core PCE will matter: a 0.3% monthly rise could lift annual core PCE back to 3.5%. That is not the disinflation the FOMC’s non -hawks were waiting for and, with these fine margins, could help to make the case for a precautionary hike given the skew to inflation risks. records.text: 8 September 2026 Focus Germany Deutsche Bank AG Page 17 While the federal states are responsible for hospital planning and investment in the healthcare sector, municipalities are often responsible for local public health offices and may operate their own municipal or city-owned hospitals. Supporting outpatient healthcare provision may also be a municipal responsibility. Municipal budgets finance public health offices and, where necessary, cover deficits incurred by municipal or city-owned hospitals. Finally, municipalities play an important role in social infrastructure. records.text: is weaker than with the PAYE data alone). We think the fall in PAYE employees (which comes from the reliable PAYE data source) and the concurrent rise in self-employment in the LFS are connected. We believe the catalyst has been the chronically high unit labour costs faced by firms, given strong nominal wage increases and costly labour-market regulation. T ogether, we think this has put upward pressure on firms’ costs and has been the tipping point in the shedding of employees. This is not an AI story. One consequence of these changes, however, may be that (a) employers have been replacing permanent employees with a more flexible (and cheaper) contract-based workforce, and/or (b) using AI, where it permits. If true, then these employee protections seem to have had the reverse effect on the very employees they were designed to shield (at least in the short-term). The unintended consequence, therefore may have been to catapult UK businesses to swiftly embrace cost-cutting AI technology—a coping mechanism for the rapidly rising labour costs. records.text: skewed to the upside, that would be the case, and indeed that is the world in which we generally see ourselves. A key focus here is geopolitical fault lines. Two of the biggest price shocks of the past decade have corresponded with a major geopolitical development (Russia invading Ukraine in 2022, the US/Iran war in 2026), and in a more fractured geopolitical environment, these kinds of events may become more frequent. Since they are more correlated with upside risks than downside, this asymmetry should naturally raise perceived inflation risk and, thus, market pricing. Of course, different geographies face different geopolitical risks/responses to higher energy prices, but we think the high-level underlying logic generally valid. For investors, the relevant point is that a structurally tighter energy system leaves less spare capacity to absorb the next shock. Put together, we see the above dynamics as supporting the argument that inflation risk premium may be underpriced. To be sure, some risks remain to the downside (AI-related disinflation risks remain real via other channels, and the ever-possible world of a broader economic slowdown), and there are meaningful additional upside risks (fiscal profligacy, de- globalization, etc.), but no discussion is complete without considering what may prove to be a secular mismatch between energy supply and demand. 8 September 2026 4 Barclays | Thinking Macro

While the higher trade barriers and precautionary stock building are ultimately aimed at improving domestic resilience, they likely also fragment global markets, reduce traded liquidity and raise price volatility. We estimate that the price impact of an external disruption (e.g. weather shock in agriculture markets) depends on its size relative to the market that absorbs it; if a regional bloc is half the size of the global market, the same shock delivers twice the price impact compared to a global market (Exhibit 12).7 Measures that lead to fragmentation can therefore generate outcomes that differ from their intended objective of managing disruption risk.8 7 The key intuition for the greater price effect in fragmented markets is that the price impact of a disruption is inversely related to the size of the market that absorbs it; if a regional bloc is half the size of the global market, the same shock delivers twice the price impact. 8 Historically—including during the 2022 energy and food crisis—governments have often responded to disruptions in essential goods by subsidizing households to ease the burden. But when many countries pursue similar measures simultaneously, the outcome can diverge from the intended objective. It is akin to a seated theater where one person stands to get a better view; soon everyone must stand, yet no one is better off than before. What makes the Tech trade increasingly risky is not the rate environment itself, but working through the source of the cash flow, or circular financing, off-balance sheet vehicles, and hyperscalers/chips companies becoming financing partners with Ban ks. Another way to think about circular financing is that fact that they are increasingly becoming a parallel credit provider, financing the purchases of their goods to corporate customers analogous to what we saw in Auto companies nearly 2 decades ago. At that time, Auto companies were the largest companies in the S&P500, and created a parallel credit system to finance demand for their own product… only the customer was the consumer then. Their downfall was that a credit crisis and systemic deleveraging hit both the earnings stream directly and the risk that had been repackaged and sold. The challenge is that the investment and trade data are reported using different classifications. BEA reports imports by type of product, whereas NIPA investment is reported by asset class. As a result, there is not always a direct import counterpart to a detailed NIPA investment category. For example, engines and turbines appear as a distinct asset within NIPA investment, but the corresponding import data are available only within a broader industrial equipment category that also includes products unrelated to hyperscaler investment. Using the broader import category could therefore overstate the import adjustment, so we do not make an adjustment for these categories at present. The resulting omission is likely to be moderate. Computers and peripherals account for roughly 60–70% of hyperscaler equipment investment and are also likely among its most import-intensive components. Our refined approach therefore captures the largest source of imported content, even though it does not capture all imported equipment used in the hyperscaler build-out.

That is, there is a very real risk that the futures curves are underpricing upside risk. More broadly, a persistent energy deficit would have implications beyond the direct contribution of energy prices to headline inflation. One of the defining features of the post-GFC period was abundant and relatively inexpensive energy, which encouraged investors and policymakers to treat energy shocks as largely transitory. An AI-driven increase in energy demand could challenge that assumption. If markets begin to view energy scarcity as a multi- year structural phenomenon, rather than a cyclical fluctuation, the result may be a higher inflation risk premium embedded in nominal yields, inflation swaps, and breakevens. There is also a convexity dynamic to watch in the inflation indices via the weight in the basket. Senators are elected indirectly, predominantly by local representatives, meaning this year’s electoral college reflects the balance produced by the March municipal elections. As we explained in a note published earlier this year, the relevant question is not whether the RN can take control of the upper Chamber – it cannot. Even a strong result would leave it in a small minority. The importance lies instead in the composition of a chamber that could become an institutional constraint under an RN presidency: constitutional changes under Article 89 require both chambers to adopt the same text. Overall, AI could weaken career formation without adversely affecting the CHIC cohort as a whole, widening income and wealth inequality over time, much as the internet and digital innovation wave did. Conventional discussions of the effects of AI on different cohorts of consumers have focused primarily on occupational exposure, often culminating in a fear of white-collar job loss. This is only one part of the story. We broaden the analysis to three channels through which AI can affect consumer spending: labor markets, financial wealth, and inflation. Across demographic groups, consumer exposures to each of these will vary. AI "exposure" is not inherently positive or negative. Greater occupational exposure, for example, could mean greater risk of displacement or larger income gains from productivity-driven wage growth. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 19 expect robotics to move slower, weighed down by hardware costs, safety requirements, heavy capital intensity, and a shortage of the real-world physical interaction data that robotics models need to train on. Our Global Robot Model projects just 35 million total robots in the US by 2030, up from 15 million in 2026, a notable increase but not enough to seriously dent the labor force, and these may well add to productivity rather than replace workers one for one. Humanoid- specific robots do not reach 1 million in the US until 2035. That longer runway gives the manual-labor cohort time to adjust, and as with agentic AI, exposure can mean augmentation, think cobots and exoskeletons, not just automation.

As long as commodity volatility sustains these earnings reversals, conventional Quality features will remain poorly aligned with market leadership. Further rate pressure should eventually favour low Leverage companies as refinancing costs rise and balance-sheet resilience becomes more valuable. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 08 September 2026 43 South Asia: tracking oil Sri Lanka and Pakistan are two countries that are some of the most impacted by the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) energy supply disruptions. As a result, their respective macro cases will likely directly depend on the evolution of energy costs as well as stabilization of supplies. The period of worst pressures appears to be largely behind for both. Sri Lanka has managed to successfully secure fuel supplies, although at a higher cost. Pakistan continues to see some supply shortages, specifically in Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG), but is turning increasingly price-sensitive, cancelling some tenders due to elevated pricing. The latter seems to indicate that fuel availability is no longer a critical issue. Inflation on the rise, but largely in check The massive fuel shock has lifted inflation in both Pakistan and Sri Lanka, which prompted 100bp hikes in both. In Sri Lanka, the headline CPI inflation remains supported by the base effect from a disinflationary 2025, which will likely keep inflation elevated throughout the year. In Pakistan, the base effect is more benign after the inflationary shock from 3Q25 floods. records.text: e capital. Surveys confirm that, unlike in energy or telecommunications infrastructure, political openness toward private ownership or a greater private -sector role is often lacking. This is particularly evident in the water sector, which has traditionally been regarded in Germany as a core element of public -service provision (Daseinsvorsorge). While private companies are involved in the operation of water supply and wastewater systems in some larger cities, the sector remains predominantly under municipal control in rural areas and is therefore highly fragmented. This fragmentation is reinforc ed by the fact that Germany has very few supra-regional water networks. Instead, smaller regional systems dominate. Similar political and public reservations exist regarding schools, childcare facilities, hospitals and municipal administrative buildings. Although private and church-affiliated providers are active in education, care and healthcare services, large-scale privatization or long-term private operating models continue to face significant opposition. Fragmented projects remain the norm Beyond the lack of political openness, another important obstacle is the small scale of many potential investment objects. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 7 A more accurate treatment of imports As we have noted in previous research, GDP accounting is different than corporate accounting. Capex spending announcements by US corporations, which have been dominated by hyperscaler spending and other merchants of compute, include all relevant spending on AI from a corporate balance sheet perspective. That said, GDP is a different measurement: it captures final spending on domestically-produced goods and services over a period of time. Estimates of GDP exclude spending on intermediate goods and imports. Put differently, GDP excludes "circular" spending between hyperscalers and spending that goes to support output abroad. A large share of hyperscaler investment consists of imported capital goods, such as semiconductors, memory, and servers. In addition, their spending plans include intermediate inputs, which do not map directly into measured investment in the national accounts. Our previous approach: Useful but limited Our previous approach estimated AI's contribution to real GDP by focusing on four categories of nonresidential business fixed investment including information processing equipment in equipment spending, software in intellectual property products, and data centers and power centers, both of which reside in structures investment. The principal obstacle is not a shortage of capital but rather the lack of investable business models. Unlike in many other European countries, Germany has only a limited number of concession or operator structures capable of generating long- term revenue streams for private investors. Motorways would theoretically be particularly attractive, as Germany possesses one of Europe’s busiest long -distance road networks. Without greater user financing or a wider application of operator models, however, this potential is likely to remain largely untapped. The state also remains the dominant actor in the rail and waterway sectors. Planned investments primarily create opportunities for construction companies, engineering service providers and technology suppliers rather than for traditional infrastructure investors. Airports constitute a partial exception, as private participation is already widespread. Nevertheless, additional investment potential appears limited because the ownership structures of major airports are already well established and many smaller airports lack sufficient profitability. As a result, institutional investors in the transport sector are often confined to indirect participation through construction and infrastructure companies or related investment funds. records.text: Cayla Seder 7 September 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General ECB preview: The ECB's p ath i s c lear u ntil g rowth b links A 25bp ECB rate hike this week is a foregone conclusion. The more important question for markets is whether the ECB can ultimately deliver the additional tightening currently priced through spring 2027. While the persistence of the Iran conflict continues to push inflation expectations higher and keep policymakers biased toward a hawkish stance, the relationship between energy prices and rate expectations has weakened as investors increasingly weigh the risk that higher commodity prices could eventually undermine growth. For now, however, those growth concerns remain largely theoretical. The Eurozone economy has proven more resilient than expected, economic surprises are comfortably positive, and real money investor flows continue to show strong EUR demand despite rising energy costs. Core inflation is likely to remain elevated in the coming months due to base effects, while inflation expectations are drifting higher across the curve, limiting the ECB's ability to sound dovish. Whether markets ultimately receive the two additional hikes currently priced will therefore depend less on inflation and more on whether higher energy costs begin to meaningfully erode economic activity. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 07/09/2026 10:44:41 GMT Distributed on: 07/09/2026 10:44:41 GMT 7 September 2026 Deutsche Bank Research Global Cross-Discipline Thematic Research Date What are the biggest market dislocations? September 2026 In the latest of our monthly “dislocations” series, we looked at what appears strange in markets, and what might be ripe for a correction. Last month we wrote about a “goldilocks” setup, where markets were pricing resilient growth, falling inflation and limited monetary tightening. We argued this was unlikely to hold, and since then, a fresh bond selloff has pushed yields to multi- year highs around the world. However, the current equilibrium remains unsustainable. That’s because rates markets still don’t reflect the extent of the inflationary pressures ahead, with only limited tightening cycles priced in. So either inflation needs to fall, or the pressure on rates will continue. And if the pressure on rates is maintained, that in turn will force an adjustment in risk assets. Something needs to give here, with several asset classes vulnerable to the impact of a more aggressive tightening cycle from central banks. records.text: 8 September 2026 Focus Germany Deutsche Bank AG Page 45 The Infrastructure Future Act adopted in 2026 has already initiated important measures aimed at accelerating procedures and speeding up the implementation of infrastructure projects. Its objective is to shorten planning and approval processes. Early public participation can also help to reduce delays. From an investor’s perspective, the often -cited requirement for “reliable regulatory frameworks” should at a minimum include the protection of acquired rights relating to projects that have already been approved or are under development. Regulatory frameworks will inevitably evolve over the coming decades across different infrastructure sectors. However, retrospective intervention in projects that have already received approval should, in principle, be avoided. These considerations are highly relevant for both private and public investors. Even highly attractive financing conditions will have only limited impact if projects cannot be realized within a reasonable timeframe. Faster planning and approval processes also reduce the risk that economic conditions change materially during the development phase, thereby undermining project viability. Well-known examples of fee -based models in Germany include water and wastewater charges. Various forms of user financing through fees also exist in the transport sector. Examples include the German truck toll, track-access charges in rail transport, and charges for using ports or airports. Revenue from ticket sales in local public passenger transport is likewise equivalent to a user charge. The same applies to charges for using electricity and gas networks in the energy market. In the healthcare sector, hospital stays are remunerated through daily rates or case- based payments that are settled through health insurers. Further examples include fees for attending childcare centers and semester contributions or tuition fees at universities or other higher-education institutions. Generally, charges for using public infrastructure should be set at a level that generates sufficient revenue to cover costs in full, without generating a profit. This is known as the cost -recovery principle. However, not least for social -policy reasons, fee levels are often set in a way that results in underfunding, for example in water services or childcare centers. The analysis is therefore intended to provide gene ral guidance. We think the fall in PAYE employees (which comes from the reliable PAYE data source) and the concurrent rise in self-employment in the LFS are connected. We believe the catalyst has been the chronically high unit labour costs faced by firms, given strong nominal wage increases and costly labour-market regulation. T ogether, we think this has put upward pressure on firms’ costs and has been the tipping point in the shedding of employees. This is not an AI story. One consequence of these changes, however, may be that (a) employers have been replacing permanent employees with a more flexible (and cheaper) contract-based workforce, and/or (b) using AI, where it permits. If true, then these employee protections seem to have had the reverse effect on the very employees they were designed to shield (at least in the short-term). The unintended consequence, therefore may have been to catapult UK businesses to swiftly embrace cost-cutting AI technology—a coping mechanism for the rapidly rising labour costs. Inflation fell to 3.5% in July, returning to the central bank’s target range as lower gasoline and diesel prices offset food and housing pressures. However, inflation is expected to rise in coming months because of fuel increases and higher food prices, while higher shipping costs and labor expenses added risks. The central bank held the policy rate at 4.5%, balancing soft domestic demand against persistent cost pressures and global uncertainty. European software leaders such as SAP and Dassault Systèmes occupy key positions within enterprise workflows. Embedding generative AI capabilities across ERP, engineering and product lifecycle management platforms could provide new avenues for growth. However, unlike infrastructure and industrial companies, AI is unlikely to drive a significant increase in debt-funded capex. Instead, the key question for investors is whether these firms can successfully defend and extend their existing franchises as AI lowers barriers to software development and introduces new competitors at the application layer. In many countries, the involvement of private capital in the financing of public infrastructure plays a greater role than it does in Germany. records.text: d-users. Electricity grids will play an even more important role, not only within countries, but also across borders. The EU will need to build long-distance grids across national borders to ensure the stable provision of electricity across Europe. Elsewhere, the Gulf Cooperation and the ASEAN economies are building cross-border grid infrastructure to strengthen their regional electricity systems. For Europe, it could also make sense to build modern grid infrastructure (ie, HVDC technology) to import solar-generated electricity from North Africa. Some projects already exist, such as the Tunisia-Sicily interconnector (ELMED), and the European Commission is studying such large- scale North African electricity imports. At the same time, Europe needs long-distance grids to move electricity from wind turbines in the North Sea further south. Distributing electricity within the continent is Europe's core challenge. As countries build out increasingly intermittent grids with higher penetration of renewables, this will increase the need for investment in grids as well as transmission and storage technologies such as transformers, switchgears and batteries. As we wrote in our Network Security series, our view is that we are on the cusp of a grid capex supercycle as investment in transmission moves closer to parity with generation, creating a potential $600bn investment opportunity. 8 September 2026 10 Barclays | Thinking Macro

records.text: d: the initial rise is due to a mismatch in skills between workers and available jobs that occurs because of rapid AI diffusion, while a further increase is because of secondary effects of weak demand after the initial shock. Even in this rapid diffusion bear case scenario, asset market moves are important, as demonstrated by the large range of potential unemployment outcomes. The most severe downturn occurs when initial labor displacement is accompanied by asset market declines. It is also possible a large and persistent enough asset market decline could cause a downturn on its own, without a labor market trigger. In this bear case, we expect the initial rise in unemployment from displacement would first affect CHIC households, as they are more exposed to AI occupationally. A decline in resources for this group would likely lead them to reduce their discretionary spend. Given the large share of spending these households control, weaker demand from this group would eventually mean the shock spreads beyond those directly exposed. Low exposure occupations tend to be more cyclical, so we expect weak demand would result in higher unemployment for these consumers as well. While the gap between these groups may narrow for a short period, all groups would be left worse off, and monetary and fiscal policy responses will be critical.

Global energy investment is expected to reach $3.4trn in 2026, up 5% year-on-year and equivalent to approximately 2.7% of global GDP (Figure 17).7 Around $2.2trn is directed towards renewables, nuclear, grids, storage, low-emissions fuels, efficiency and electrification, versus $1.2trn for oil, natural gas and coal. Hence, electricity-related capital spending now represents nearly 60% of total energy investments, reflecting the growing needs from generation into grids, storage and end-use electrification. Such investment expenditure into energy (ie, not the total energy 'bill' nor the energy sector's value added) had already been around 3% about a decade ago. It then fell during 2015-19 (towards 2.5%), as the post-2014 oil price fall sharply reduced fossil-fuel capex, which was not fully offset by increased spending on clean-energy. With the onset of COVID in 2020, it temporarily dropped even further, before returning to close to 3% in 2025/26. Going further back into history, data becomes less reliable.8 Typically, however, energy investments were relatively closely aligned with the price of oil, which incentivised investment activity in an oil- dominated energy system. ECB—Has R* Risen Further? The equilibrium policy rate—the rate at which the economy is in balance with inflation at target, often called r*—is back in focus, as some ECB officials have argued that monetary policy should turn mildly restrictive. The equilibrium rate is unobserved and very difficult to measure, but potentially an important input into monetary policymaking. The ECB staff estimated in early 2024 that the equilibrium rate had risen since the pre-Covid period, with the nominal neutral rate rising into a 1.75-2.25% range. ECB officials have recently suggested that the upper end of this range might have drifted up to 2.5%, with some Council members suggesting that r* could be even higher than that. Daniel Gerard September 8th, 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General Classification: Complimentary Material Should Higher Rates Scare Equities? It’s complicated While there are many present and pending threats to asset performance, institutional investors - in their holdings and behaviour at least - remain unconcerned. Global equities continue to perform just fine. In aggregate, institutional investors remain sanguine. They are holding record equity positions, and are increasingly shunning duration as a hedge, with overweights highly concen trated in large cap US growth. Yet one of the most frequent discussions we have with our clients is what impact higher rates has on this puzzle? While various rate regimes are often used as strawmen in this debate, we need to recognize that it’s why rates are high/moving higher that matters. The period we are currently in is drastically different from others over the past few decades, so much so, that we can almost throw the comparisons out of the rolling 3y moving average window. So how will the level of rates impact equity markets this time around? Perhaps the best way to begin is by throwing out the premise. records.text: M Foundation 2 Executive Summary: Building a better mousetrap to estimate the contribution of AI spending on growth Understanding the outlook for the US economy increasingly requires understanding AI spending and how it permeates the National Income and Product Accounts. While we have long sought to understand AI and its economic effects, the evolution of the AI investment cycle has created an opportunity to refine how we track its contribution to US GDP growth. In particular, we enhance our framework along three dimensions: the treatment of imports, the separation of AI from non-AI spending, and the distinction between spending on AI infrastructure build-out and AI adoption. Our refined methodology provides a more comprehensive view of how AI spending is flowing through the US economy. It extends beyond the technology-focused categories at the center of our original estimates, to capture the broader infrastructure required to build AI capacity. Under this broader definition, we estimate that AI-related investment has contributed 0.6pp to annualized real GDP growth on average since 2025. Narrowing the lens to isolate AI-only investment still produces a sizable 0.4pp contribution. The framework also allows us to distinguish between the infrastructure build-out and AI adoption, providing a way to track the AI cycle as it moves from capacity creation to broader diffusion across the economy. records.text: 8 September 2026 Focus Germany Deutsche Bank AG Page 28 Figure 8: Higher investment in electricity grids Source: Federal Network Agency Particularly in the transmission grid segment, project sizes are well suited to institutional investors. Concrete examples already exist of investors acquiring stakes in German electricity networks. One prominent case is the sale of the German TenneT electricity network through a multi -investor transaction. The German federal government, through development bank KfW, acquired a 25.1% stake in TenneT Germany for approximately EUR 3.3 bn. In addition, three international institutional investors committed a combined EUR 9.5 bn in equity capital and together acquired 46% of the German network: the Dutch pension fund APG, the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund NBIM and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC. The Dutch state retained the remaining 28.9% through the original TenneT Holding structure. This example demonstrates that institutional investors participate in German electricity infrastructure not only through debt financing but also by providing direct equity capital. Electricity networks therefore belong to those segments of Germany’s energy infrastructure where institutional capital is already being mobilized in very concrete ways. The investment requirement is also substantial in electricity distribution networks. Phosphate fertilizers4, by contrast, can be drawn down from soil reserves in the n short term, limiting the immediate impact on yields, but sustained under‑application depletes these reserves and gradually weakens soil quality, crop resilience, and productivity. This is particularly relevant in Brazil soybeans (accounting for 62% of global exports), where import dependence on phosphate fertilizers is high (~80%). We also expect growth to notch higher in India in 2026 (50bp upward revision) on stronger than expected high frequency data. records.text: 7 September 2026 Thematic Research Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG n If we look at market pricing for the June 2027 meeting, it’s seen little movement from its peak on July 23, the same day that Brent closed above $100/bbl again. Back then, it was pricing 74bps of further hikes by the June 2027 meeting, and at time of writing, it’s pricing in 72bps of further hikes. n Yet in that time, natural gas futures have risen significantly, up more than +18%. Brent is almost level again at $96/bbl, the growth data has continuously surprised on the upside, and even investor expectations of inflation have risen significantly. So in other words, the newsflow and market pricing for inflation has shifted hawkishly, yet ECB pricing hasn’t. n Looking forward, we know that further inflationary pressures remain in the pipeline, and central banks also tend to overcorrect for perceived mistakes in the last cycle. In the ECB’s case, they came under criticism for reacting too late to the 2021-22 inflation shock, as they didn’t even begin to lift the deposit rate out of negative territory until inflation was above 8%. This year, however, we saw how they already delivered a rate hike in June, even though headline CPI was “only” at +2.8% that month. records.text: 2 Insights About State Street PriceStats PriceStats is a source of high frequency inflation information drawn from prices of over five million items sold by online retailers. The items include food, beverages, electronics, apparel, furniture, household products, prescription drugs and over-the-counter medicines. The prices are collated for all the countries we monitor to produce individual Country Inflation Series. Country Inflation Series detect changes in inflation trends with real-time data. We publish the indices with a lag of three business days; they are direct reflections of the prices of real products on sale at online retailers in each country. Country Inflation Series are not seasonally adjusted and are not designed to match official data. The interactive Country Inflation Series charts overlay against the relevant official measures of inflation, in all cases non-seasonally adjusted. records.text: AI-related overinvestment could bring a downturn. CHIC households, and especially older CHIC households, have more equity exposure, both in absolute terms and as a share of their own net worth. The top 20% income cohort, the college-educated group, and the 55+ age group all account for around 80+% of equity exposure among households. Among lower-income and less-educated households, a smaller share have any equity exposure at all. As a result, changes in equity valuations can more easily drive changes in net worth, and thus changes in spending, for CHIC households. The final transmission channel we consider is through inflation: Near-term demand pressures from AI could lead to higher prices, but in the longer-term, productivity gains could result in disinflation. We expect electricity, software, and chip-related goods to drive near-term AI-related price pressures, even if those pressures are somewhat limited. Given these categories (especially electricity) make up larger shares of spending for low-income, less-educated, and younger households, these groups are likely more exposed. Meanwhile, if longer-term disinflation first stems from industries with higher adoption rates, and thus materializes in services categories such as financial and communication services, higher-income households will benefit first.

When an SSW disrupts the polar vortex, it weakens the westerly winds that normally shield northwestern Europe from Arctic air, allowing cold Siberian air masses to pour in from the east, while simultaneously suppressing North Sea wind generation. This creates a concurrent spike in heating demand and collapse in wind output – a key upside risk to our otherwise bearish European power prices in Q1 2027. France would likely be more shielded from a cold spell than Germany due to strong nuclear availability, though increased pull from interconnector flows would still see significant upside to its power prices in a cold spell. 2027 looks overbought: We see European power balances improving beyond the winter, driven by significantly looser global gas fundamentals and the end of El Niño weather patterns. Tail risks remain, though, with potential upside risks from Middle East conflict escalations, slow recovery of hydro stocks and extreme weather (both in summer and winter). records.text: 8 Japan Research | 08 September 2026 Japan equity strategy: Toward a stronger yen and higher equities Masashi Akutsu >> BofAS Japan masashi.akutsu@bofa.com This was my fourth BofA Japan Conference – and also the busiest. Roughly half of this reflected (1) growing and more firmly established interest in Japanese equities, while the other half stemmed from (2) investor questions about the uncertain macro environment and the implications for stock selection. Regarding (1), Japan’s inflationary environment and corporate reforms, which began in 2023, have now entered their fourth year, attracting a broader range of investors to Japanese equities. We met with many long-term investors from the US, Europe, the Middle East and other regions. Discussions focused on Japan’s structural transformation and its relative attractiveness versus other markets. Many investors were keen to identify undervalued stocks from a medium-term perspective. We explained that while the phase of rapid acceleration in corporate reforms has largely run its course, Japan is now entering a stage in which ROE should rise steadily. Since the start of corporate reforms in 2023, participation by Asian investors, who are geographically and culturally closer to Japan, increased sharply. Since 2H last year, however, as improvements in ROE have become more visible, interest from investors in other regions has also continued to grow. records.text: 42 08 September 2026 Figure 57: Tier-1 cities – secondary home price index, an indicator of core-city rather than nationwide stabilization Source: NBS, Centaline On 28 August, the Ministry of Housing and Urban-Rural Development of China issued a notice to phase out, but not eliminate, the pre-sales system. The main downside shock is the PBOC’s requirement that banks may not release pre-sales proceeds to developers until project completion. Primary sales volumes may drop further as developers face slower cash collection, weaker land-banking appetite, and potentially lower sales growth/ROE (partly offset by relaxed funding channels). Our China property analysts believe that this is directionally positive for the housing market, as reduced supply may help stabilize home prices, an important precondition for a sustainable recovery, and the measures support market consolidation, particularly SOE developments with strong balance sheets (e.g. COLI, CRL). However, over the near- term, developers (especially smaller ones) are adversely impacted from a growth perspective. Local governments may also see weaker land sales revenue. Potential beneficiaries are: (1) KE Holdings (covered by Daniel Chen), as lower primary supply may boost secondary volumes; and (2) homebuyers, as mortgage tenors extend from 30 to 40 years, although the boost to sales may be limited (see China Property & Banks: Phasing out the pre-sales system - good or bad?, Karl Chan & Katherine Lei, 29 Aug). Accounting for the higher base for comparison in 2H26 but lagged impact from higher global prices, we expect year-on- year inflation to moderate modestly, albeit it would still be above policy target in majority of economies. Going ahead, we still see considerable amount of upside risks. First, volatility in energy markets could persist in the near term. Crude oil prices have rebounded again since mid-August amid the resurgence of US-Iran tensions, with Brent trading above $90/barrel once again. Our BofA Global Commodities Team projects Brent price to average $103/b assuming partial re-opening (30-50% of normal flow), or US$120/b assuming fragile ceasefire with ongoing tensions (<30% of normal flow). Second, elevated crack spread (i.e. cost of converting crude oil to refined products), could imply broader inflationary impact. The Singapore gasoil 10ppm, benchmark price for sulphur diesel in the largest trading hub in Asia, stood elevated at $150/barrel despite Dubai crude oil price has peaked out (Exhibit 7), reflecting the supply constraint on refinery capacity, such as that in the Middle East and Russia. Such elevated crack spread would translate to higher cost for producers, and eventually to consumers, barring additional relief measures.

Smaller rooftop systems, which account for the majority of PV installations in Germany, are less suitable for direct institutional investment. Most new rooftop systems, often combined with battery storage, are primarily designed for self - consumption and fi nanced by the user. In addition, the administrative effort required to monitor and manage a large number of dispersed assets is substantial for individual investments. Nevertheless, the potential of smaller PV installations can also be made accessible to institutional investors through project aggregation. In such cases, numerous rooftop and ground -mounted systems are consolidated into a single portfolio. Legally, these assets can be grouped under a common project company. This approach significantly reduces administrative burdens for investors because they interact with only one central entity. At the same time, bundling creates broad risk diversification: technical failures or lower yields from individual installations can be offset through the overall performance of the portfolio. Certain asset managers have specialised in structuring, building and professionally managing such portfolios for large investors and family offices. These service providers handle project sourcing, technical and commercial operations, and electricity marketing. A refined treatment of imports part 3: Including semiconductors and related devices Finally, we broaden the import adjustment to include semiconductors and related devices, which are also an important input into AI investment. Although the supply of chips and memory, and the associated inflationary pressures, have been widely discussed this year, the dollar value of imported semiconductors and related devices remains much smaller than imports of computers and peripherals, both in nominal and real terms. Moreover, imports of semiconductors and related devices did not accelerate until 4Q25, two years later than imports of computers, peripherals and parts. Their subsequent growth, however, has been significant—averaging a 57% annual rate in 1H26—and, together with the discussion around "chipflation," makes accounting for them increasingly important. As an approximation, we assume that these imports are used entirely for private fixed investment, as households and governments are more likely to purchase final computing devices than semiconductors themselves. This refinement better captures the imported content of building AI hyperscalers than relying on computers and peripherals alone. For institutional investors, regional platform models that bundle multiple deployment projects and thereby achieve the required scale are particularly attractive. Data centers currently represent the most dynamic sub -segment. They benefit from growing demand for computing capacity driven by AI and cloud applications. Large -scale facilities with long -term tenancy agreements fit well with the requirements of many inst itutional investors. At present, the main risks are less related to demand and more to permitting procedures, land availability and, above all, access to sufficient electricity-grid capacity. Overall, digital infrastructure is characterized by a high degree of political openness, private -sector market structures and attractive growth prospects. Institutional capital is frequently deployed alongside strategic investors, which take responsibility for operational management. Transport Infrastructure Compared with energy and digital infrastructure, the transport sector exhibits substantial investment requirements but offers considerably fewer opportunities for institutional investors. Roads, railways, waterways and other elements of transport infrastru cture remain largely under public -sector responsibility in Germany. But later announced a “fiscal adjustment bill” that will aim to narrow the deficit by 2.2pp of GDP in 2027. The content of the bill is yet to be revealed and voted in Congress. Our expectation is the bill gets approved, but in a diluted form (~1.5pp). At the current juncture, what happens with fiscal policy is highly relevant to predict the central bank’s next steps. Inflation is above the tolerance range for the sixth year in a row. The central bank (BanRep) blames expansionary fiscal policy, the 50% increase in the minimum wage over four years, and other supply shocks for the high and sticky inflation. If the government provides convincing signals that a meaningful fiscal adjustment is coming, we think BanRep will start cutting rates in 2027. However, before that, another supply shock, El Niño, seems inescapable. In a previous report (see report: El Niño comes with inflation under his arm) we estimated Colombia is the Latam country with the highest inflation sensitivity to El Niño, mainly propagated through food and electricity. That’s why we have an out-of-consensus call on rates: 100bp on hikes before the end of 2026 (October and December, 50bp each) vis-à-vis marketing pricing ~40bp.

Building on our previous productivity analysis from earlier this year, we show further evidence that, whilst the pick-up is broad-based, it is primarily driven by the “white collar” sector (excluding finance). Data centers therefore offer a relatively direct route into digital infrastructure and often involve project sizes that match the requirements of major institutional investors. At the same time, the risks differ from those associated with traditional network investments. Data centers require large sites, reliable electricity supplies and increasingly sophisticated concepts for the utilization of waste heat. One of the most important bottlenecks is access to high -capacity power connections . In many areas of Germany, local distribution networks are currently unable to accommodate the substantial electricity demand associated with modern data centers. As a result, some projects fail to obtain approval. In addition to constraints in the power grid, lengthy permitting procedures and scarcity of suitable land represent major obstacles to future market growth. Figure 4 illustrates the extent of the rebound from the March low and how the rise has extended across the summer. This rise in funding ratios reduces unwind needs across transition. When funds make the transition to the new scheme, they move from hedging liabilities to investing assets. Thus, when funds hold more assets relative to liabilities this reduces unwind needs across transition. For example, if a fund had a 70% hedge ratio in the current scheme and a target hedge ratio of 50% in the new scheme, at a 100% funding ratio that would represent a 20% decline. However, at a 120% funding ratio, that would only result in a 10% decline (70% - 50%*120%).
