However, this should not affect the MPC's decision on QT as the level of reserves is a question about the BoE's liabilities and is determined by market demand. QT , on the other hand, is largely a question about how the BoE manages the assets that back those liabilities, and therefore the composition can be shifted (fewer bonds held outright, more repos) without changing the aggregate balance sheet size. MPC members have repeatedly been clear that the MPC can, in theory, reduce the APF gilt holdings to zero, even if reserves demand remains high. In fact, BoE staff have expressed an aim that the majority of reserves will be backed with repo, in part to reduce interest rate risk on the balance sheet, which would imply the current c.£488bn of gilt holdings is far in excess of the ultimate steady state. QT is pushing up gilt yields. The MPC's assessment in July found this to be true and, in fact, revised slightly upward its estimate, to 20-30bp. At present, there is no clear political initiative aimed at extending such models across the mot orway network. At the same time, the introduction of a car toll on federal motorways is not currently under consideration. In principle, the potential for operator models on German motorways is considerable. records.text: s. Transfers and general -purpose allocations from the states under the municipal fiscal-equalization system are another source of finance. These funds are intended to provide a basic level of funding for the performance of mandatory tasks and to compensate for regional disparities. Counties also receive earmarked transfers for specific areas of responsibility or funding programs. Counties are frequently the public authorities responsible for local public transport. In this capacity, they commission local public transport services from transport companies in order to improve mobility for the population within the county. School transport is an important component of these services. In addition to ticket revenue, the principal sources of finance are grants from the federal government and the states. Under the Municipal Transport Financing Act, for example, the federal government provides funding for the expansion and improvement of local public transport infrastructure. Specific funding programs may also be used, for instance to purchase electric buses or digitize trans port services. Municipalities are particularly important in utility and waste -disposal infrastructure, which are among the traditional areas of public -service provision. records.text: rmal again in yield terms rather than being extreme. Today's CoTD highlights one way of viewing that adjustment. Since the early 1960s, 10-year Treasury yields have broadly tracked a rolling 10-year average of nominal GDP growth, with two notable exceptions: the late 1970s and early 1980s, when yields moved well above nominal growth, and the 2010s, when they sat meaningfully below it. Over the full period, nominal GDP has exceeded 10- year yields by an average of around 70bps. Given a current 10-year average nominal GDP growth rate of roughly 5.5%, that points to a 'fair' yield of around 4.8%, exactly where we are today. However, that’s a 10-year moving average. Current nominal GDP growth is running at 6.6% YoY, the strongest pace since 2005 outside of the post-Covid rebound. So should yields be higher? In Q2, nominal growth was boosted by the energy shock so that seems a little extreme, unless it becomes permanent, but maybe with the AI boom, and inflation which has been stubbornly above target for over 5 years, perhaps nominal GDP should currently be moving above its 10-year moving average, thus dragging yields higher. That said, it’s certainly not all bad news. As discussed in last Wednesday's CoTD and reiterated in the pack, 10-year Treasuries would still generate a positive 12- month total return provided yields remain below roughly 5.5% over the next year. However, under the above scenario, it would be necessary to monitor increases in deposit beta, credit costs, and the pace of expansion in bond loss cuts. (3) Views of investors who indicated downside risks: Some investors commented that if the policy rate differential between the US and Japan narrows going forward and the yen appreciates to below ¥150 against the dollar, there is a risk that the pace of BoJ rate hikes will not accelerate as much as the market expects and the terminal rate will decline to around 1.50-1.75%. In this case, given that the market has already fully priced in a policy rate of 1.75%, some investors pointed out that downward pressure would arise on forecast ROE / valuations for bank stocks, strengthening the underperforming trend in bank stocks.

records.text: 2) Uneven revenue and margin recovery Revenue growth accelerated further in 1H26 as reflation took hold, but the n recovery remained highly uneven across sectors. Aggregate revenue for the All-China listed universe grew 6% yoy in 1H26, up from 2% in 2025 and -1% in 2024. The improvement was driven primarily by upstream sectors benefiting from improving PPI and margin recovery, with Materials (+15%) and Energy (+6%) showing a clear recovery in pricing, while IT (+22%) and Financials (+13%) also remained strong. In contrast, downstream consumer sectors continued to lag, with revenue growth of only 2–4% across Consumer cohorts, reflecting still-soft household demand and subdued CPI inflation. Aggregate net margin for the All-China universe improved to 8.2% in 1H26 from n 7.6% in 1H25. Margin expansion was most pronounced in sectors experiencing both revenue acceleration and improving pricing power underpinned by operating leverage, including IT (6.7% vs. 3.6%), Materials (6.1% vs. 4.1% in 1H25), and Brokers (40% vs. 31%). records.text: 5) AI starting to fuel a Capex upcycle China’s listed universe is showing signs of a Capex upcycle, with aggregate Capex n growth for the ex-financial universe accelerating to +8% yoy in 1H26 from +1% in FY25. Capex intensity also moved higher to 7.3% in 1H26 from 7.0% in 1H25. The recovery has been led primarily by AI-related sectors. IT (+18% yoy), Communication Services (+20%), and Industrials (+14%) recorded the strongest Capex growth in 1H26, reflecting continued investment in AI infrastructure, cloud computing, data centers, semiconductors and advanced manufacturing. Consensus expectations for AI Capex growth have also moved higher following n the 2Q/1H26 earnings season. The Chinese AI universe has seen forward Capex estimates revised up by 8% over the past month, driven primarily by (listed) hyperscalers, whose Capex forecasts have been revised up by 34%. This represents the largest one-month Capex upward revision since the “DeepSeek Moment” in February 2025. Inventory growth has also accelerated alongside capex expansion in these sectors n (IT and Communication Services +29%/+11%), suggesting active capacity build-out and procurement ahead of expected demand. In contrast, traditional sectors remain more cautious. Capex intensity declined in n Energy (7.4% in 1H26 vs. 8.4% in 1H25), Materials (5.8% vs. 6.6%), and Consumer Staples (4.0% vs. 4.5%). records.text: ■ Framing the summer selloff in bonds. It was a tough summer for government bonds, with yields touching multi-decade highs globally. US Treasury interventions and Fed expectation management have had only a modest impact. The synchronous rise in global bond yield levels remains an important consideration, but the rates curves point to significant regional divergence. In the US, 2s10s steepened by nearly 25bp in August before retracing half the move post Jackson Hole. Long-end volatility has been the main theme in the US reflecting the contest around the Fed’s inflation control credentials and hyperscaler bond supply. ■ In Europe, the yield curve has seen more of a parallel shift and the rates volatility is still primarily a policy rate story which by extension is a natural gas story. With the market now pricing in 45-50bp of rate hikes through the remainder of the year, the pricing tension at the long end is less pronounced. Our European rates colleagues therefore see little justification in “selling” Bunds at current levels (see The last of the robust hikes?). records.text: 1. Macro and Rates – Crediting past performance and economic resilience ■ European credit outperformance versus other major fixed income assets likely to continue. A notable feature of the higher yield regime over the past year has been the resilience of credit. Since July 2022, when the ECB first hiked rates in this cycle, the Bloomberg corporate index has generated total returns of 10.7% cumulatively – well above the -2.5% in sovereigns and c2% in the government-related subindices of the Bloomberg aggregate. More importantly, the returns volatility also weighs in favor of corporate bonds. We expect this set-up to remain intact over the coming months. ■ Economic endurance likely to keep flows into credit steady. European economies have weathered the energy price and trade tensions well thus far. Our economists attribute this resilience to (1) global stockpiling in anticipation of future price hikes and (2) a synchronized investment cycle across exported oriented and domestic segments. Overall, they see Eurozone GDP growth at ~1% this year and accelerating to 1.5% in 2027 (see Back to School). ■ We see this combination of range-bound yields and steady growth as supportive for credit market performance. 4 Yield seeking flows into credit have been supported by economic resilience in Europe Citi Research, Bloomberg Corporate credit has delivered better returns with lower volatility -100 -80 -60 -40 -20 0 20 40 60 80 100 Sep-21 Mar-22 Sep-22 Mar-23 Sep-23 Mar-24 Sep-24 Mar-25 Sep

Unlike many other European countries, however, Germany lacks the political preconditions for the widespread use of concession and operator models based on user charges or availability payments. As long as financing and operation remain predominantly organized by the state and no user -financed car -toll system is introduced, transport infrastructure in Germany will continue to be primarily a publicly financed investment field. This highlights a broader dilemma. The federal government is planning significantly higher investment precisely in those infrastructure sectors where direct participation by private capital remains politically constrained. This applies especially to motorw ays, federal highways, railways and waterways, where the state retains primary responsibility for financing and operation. The planned increase in public spending will nevertheless create significant market opportunities along the value chain, including for construction companies, engineering service providers, building -materials manufacturers and suppliers of infrastructure t echnology. The legislation follows President Trump’s January 2026 directive for GSEs to purchase $200bn of agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS) to improve housing affordability by supporting lower mortgage rates for 30Y fixed-rate loans. Despite these policy initiatives, we see little near-term relief in sight for the supply-demand mismatch. Restrictions on land use and housing construction, along with higher construction costs and labor shortages in building trades, are constraining supply. Mortgage rates are 70bps higher than the lows observed a year ago, while valuations are stretched in certain geographies. Our economics team notes that absent accompanying measures to increase supply, measures that boost demand—such as lower mortgage rates or down payment assistance—tend to push prices higher over time, making them an unsustainable solution for long-term affordability. records.text: Higher barriers to trade may lower barriers to shocks because: 1. Small supply shocks can trigger much larger losses of exportable supply. With global agriculture trade highly concentrated among a handful of major exporters, a small physical disruption — or even the risk of one — in a key exporting country can trigger (precautionary) export restrictions that remove far more supply from the global markets than the original disruption itself (Exhibit 11). During the food price crises of 2008 and 2022, successive export bans on grains and edible oils amplified global price spikes. India’s rice export ban ahead of the 2023/24 strong El Niño removed about 40% of global rice trade from export markets and contributed to a sharp increase in prices, even though Indian rice production ultimately proved resilient. Fiscal easing is back? The Ministry of Finance has stated that the government is planning to increase transfers from the Oil Fund by KZT1.5trn starting from 2027 to finance strategic investment projects. The move marks notable fiscal easing, which partly reverses 2026 consolidation, which could potentially compromise disinflation trend and reduce the scope for the expected rate cuts. However, taking into account broader fiscal plans, we think longer term disinflation trend is likely to still remain in place as potential fiscal easing is unlikely to be material. Thus, KZT1.5trn in additional Oil Fund spending is equivalent to around 0.7% of GDP. At the same time, the government continues to plan to cut broader budget deficit from 2.5% of GDP in 2026 to 2.3% in 2027 and falling further to 0.9% of GDP by 2029. If these plans will be sustained, this consolidation is likely to be more than sufficient to offset rising Oil Fund spending and keep inflation on a steady downward trend. However, we also admit that any major potential changes of the fiscal policy path pose the key fundamental risk to the expected disinflation/monetary easing cycle.

records.text: UK Economics 07 September 2026 Citi Research 2 Since the Global Financial Crisis, the UK has been marred by poor productivity growth. Competing theories from academics and policymakers have been put forth to ascribe the causes of the UK Productivity Puzzle (e.g. See Barnett et al, 2014, or Van Reenen and Yang, 2024), but none have fully dominated the narrative. Now, the reverse appears to be happening. By some measures, UK productivity growth is finally picking up, and in a meaningful way too. Building on our previous productivity analysis from earlier this year, we show further evidence that, whilst the pick-up is broad-based, it is primarily driven by the “white collar” sector (excluding finance). This sector has the clearest productivity enhancing benefits from AI advancements. It is most obvious in the ICT sector, where cumulative productivity growth since 2022 is 32% (using HMRC’s PAYE measure). However, this finding is sensitive to the data used and the comparison points. Whilst—by some measures—the pick-up in sectoral productivity has been broad, it really depends on the vantage-point. Namely, first, the time-period being examined and, second, the variables used to calculate measured productivity. Productivity has grown inconsistently, so different starting points can yield different outcomes. 8 September 2026 Focus Germany Deutsche Bank AG Page 8 infrastructure assets may be financed through a different model from their subsequent operation. Tax financing Tax financing is particularly suitable for infrastructure that cannot be operated on a commercially viable basis, or where commercially viable operation is not pursued or desired for political reasons. In Germany, this applies, for example, to most roads, railway infrastructure, educational facilities, hospitals and public properties. In many cases, the operation of public infrastructure facilities is subsidised by tax revenue. As a rule , the principle of non-affectation principle applies: Specific taxes are not earmarked for individual infrastructure segments. Fees and user financing Unlike tax financing, financing infrastructure facilities through fees generally involves the earmarking of revenue. Users pay a fee for using the infrastructure, and the revenue from these fees is used for the benefit of the respective infrastructure assets. This reflects the principle of equivalence . Fee -based financing requires that, in principle, all users can be required to contribute to the financing, or that it is possible to prevent the infrastructure concerned from being used without payment of a fee, thereby avoiding free -riding. records.text: t. In the base case outcome described above, CHIC households benefit most. These consumers ultimately experience the largest increase in resources due to their higher exposures to equity prices, productivity gains, new tasks, and disinflation. Within this group, some consumers (potentially younger households, who are more exposed to displacement and less exposed to asset markets) might be worse-off in the short-term, but others will be better off. Overall, spending for this cohort rises most and income and wealth inequality widen, as was the case in prior innovation waves. Given these CHIC households account for a large portion of consumer spending, positive outcomes for this group as a whole mean that the overall drag on spending from displacement should be more modest. CHIC households also drive even larger shares of discretionary spending categories, including big-ticket items like furniture and vehicles, luxury goods, and recreational services such as entertainment. Our positive outlook for the high-end consumer means spending in these discretionary spending categories should remain robust.

records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 07 Sep 2026 02:00:00 ET │ 13 pages UK Economics The new Productivity Puzzle and the AI structural shift CITI'S TAKE Since the GFC, UK productivity growth has been poor. Various theories have been put forward to explain this pattern, but none have fully described the problem. It now appears we have the reverse. By some metrics, UK productivity growth is finally on the rise. Building on our productivity analysis from earlier this year, we show evidence it is primarily driven by ICT, although other sectors that benefit from AI advancements also play a role. We think this development is both positive and meaningful, although we remain cautious. The UK is experiencing a new productivity puzzle — After 15 years of sluggish productivity growth (let’s call it the “OG” productivity puzzle), the opposite is finally happening, although the causes of this boost to productivity are not yet fully clear. We think this is a meaningful shift, but it is sensitive to the data used — The improvement is best seen when using HMRC’s RTI (PAYE) data. Annual productivity growth averaged 1.2% per quarter since 2024Q3. The white-collar sector is leading the way, and ICT is the flag bearer — Since 2025, ICT contributed over a third of the annual productivity (PAYE) growth, despite comprising less than 10% of the entire economy. We think the productivity boost is correlated with ICT’s pervasive use of AI

Investor sentiment toward the sector appears to be gradually improving. As interest in AI- and semiconductor-related stocks, which have been key drivers of the Japanese equity market, has moderated somewhat, we are beginning to see signs of capital rotating into the biopharma sector, which has relatively underperformed. In particular, both domestic and international investors showed strong interest in companies that combine solid earnings growth from existing products with the potential for long-term value creation through late-stage pipeline assets. At the same time, investor focus is gradually shifting from revenue growth to earnings growth. While expectations for continued top-line expansion from key products remain high across the sector, a key question is how effectively companies can translate that growth into sustainable profit expansion. Investors also remain highly focused on the next generation of growth drivers. records.text: noted in the report referenced above, energy demand is rising faster than supply at the same time as geopolitical fragmentation is increasing the premium on energy security, creating a complex terrain for global investors to navigate. Key question: does the upside inflation risk from the energy supply/demand imbalance overwhelm other disinflationary forces? This creates a tension in the market narrative. For several months/quarters now, the inflation discourse has gravitated toward the idea that AI is near-term inflationary but medium-term disinflationary (for instance, see A Claudy inflation outlook for our thinking on the topic back in March, and Inflation has a memory problem, where we explore one facet of AI-related inflation). But what if this is wrong, or at a minimum, overly simplistic? While we still strongly sympathize with that framework on a basic level, a more nuanced take would need to acknowledge that the path to any eventual productivity dividend may itself be energy and commodity intensive. The focus of this note is therefore on a growing upside risk that may be underappreciated in inflation pricing: energy. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 08 September 2026 31 We think the recalibration of the policy mix was instrumental in containing the macro- financial stability risks triggered by the war. The Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT) tightened the monetary stance through a 300bp increase in the effective funding rate and tighter loan-growth caps, with lower limits and narrower exemptions. Tighter financial conditions and the slightly faster pace of depreciation helped contain non-energy imports as higher energy imports widened the current account deficit. records.text: skewed to the upside, that would be the case, and indeed that is the world in which we generally see ourselves. A key focus here is geopolitical fault lines. Two of the biggest price shocks of the past decade have corresponded with a major geopolitical development (Russia invading Ukraine in 2022, the US/Iran war in 2026), and in a more fractured geopolitical environment, these kinds of events may become more frequent. Since they are more correlated with upside risks than downside, this asymmetry should naturally raise perceived inflation risk and, thus, market pricing. Of course, different geographies face different geopolitical risks/responses to higher energy prices, but we think the high-level underlying logic generally valid. For investors, the relevant point is that a structurally tighter energy system leaves less spare capacity to absorb the next shock. Put together, we see the above dynamics as supporting the argument that inflation risk premium may be underpriced. To be sure, some risks remain to the downside (AI-related disinflation risks remain real via other channels, and the ever-possible world of a broader economic slowdown), and there are meaningful additional upside risks (fiscal profligacy, de- globalization, etc.), but no discussion is complete without considering what may prove to be a secular mismatch between energy supply and demand. 8 September 2026 4 Barclays | Thinking Macro

records.text: hat gets built and where, as underwriting rules and claims decisions can determine whether a building or neighborhood is viewed as insurable enough to justify renovations, upgrades, or retrofits. This results in many operators delaying building improvements, sometimes indefinitely. The Federal Reserve’s analysis, Rising Property Insurance Costs and Pass-Through to Rents for Apartment Buildings, looks at whether landlords pass higher insurance costs on to tenants by tracking changes in rental revenue, asking rents, and other expenses alongside insurance increases. They find that rental revenues tend to rise when insurance costs rise, but asking rents don’t move with insurance costs, implying the revenue effect may come more from increases paid by existing tenants rather than from higher rents on new leases. Each $1 increase in insurance costs lowers net income by about $0.72, meaning owners bear most of the burden, and tenants pay a small share on average, an estimated $7–$12 more per month since 2019. The Minneapolis Fed survey of multifamily housing owners similarly indicated that rising insurance costs are increasing financial vulnerability of multifamily housing. Affordable housing providers that have accepted public funding have less flexibility to increase rents or reduce property insurance coverage to mitigate higher premiums than market-rate owners. records.text: 27 08 September 2026 6. Generational divides are widening as household formation is delayed. Housing costs have risen faster than incomes, leading more young adults to remain at home. Realtor.com research estimates that in 2025, nearly 1 in 3 young adults under the age of 35 live with their parents, just below the pandemic peak. This is also consistent with research from the Urban Institute showing that about 20% of Americans ages 25-34 live with their parents. If the early 2000s trend had continued, nearly 5mn fewer young adults would be living at home today. The economics of independent living are increasingly strained as 70% of employed 25-34 year olds live at home with their parents. Rents are highest where young adults are most likely to remain in their parents’ homes, and this pattern holds across income levels, especially for lower-income households. In high-cost metros, the share of young adults living with their parents exceeds that of low-cost metros by 5.8%-pts, a gap that was non-existent in 2005. Among the lowest-income young adults in high-cost metros, the share living with parents rose by 16.4%-pts over this period. The Pew Research Center points out that 9 in 10 adults younger than 40 (89%) say it’s harder for young adults today to buy a home than it was for their parents’ generation. This backdrop of a changing world order, rapid technology change, an uneven geographical distribution of natural resources, and rapidly rising global electricity needs, has now put energy at the centre of today's geo-economics. Facing a MESS: Molecules, Electrons, Science, Security Securing the flow of molecules In a world that for the foreseeable future still needs hydrocarbons, the traditional quest to secure the flow of these molecules remains. Hence, an important part of geo-economics is still about who exports and imports the physical commodities of oil and natural gas, who refines petroleum products, and how reliable the associated supply chains are. The rise in geopolitical conflicts has led to energy importers diversifying their supply chains across geographies and infrastructures (eg, pipeline gas and LNG). In addition, importing countries also consider increasing their storage capacity of fossil fuels. The ongoing supply disruption from the Iran war has powerfully demonstrated the effectiveness of such strategies. records.text: M Foundation 10 To organize our analysis, we focus on three key transmission channels, each of which plays an important role in the general equilibrium model: 1 1) Labor markets. AI can affect labor markets in several ways. First, it could be possible that some tasks are cheaper to perform with AI rather than human labor, and if so, this could lead to labor displacement. Second, AI could enhance consumers' productivity, allowing them to produce more output with the same number of hours worked. If so, this could lead to stronger wage growth. Third, new tasks and jobs could be created related to AI, increasing employment in certain industries or creating new industries entirely. For consumers: The net effect of these three forces will determine total labor income, the main driver of spending. If the income lost due to labor displacement is larger than the income gained from productivity-driven wage growth and new jobs, then labor income will decline, but the opposite could be true as well. 2) Wealth. If AI boosts productivity, firms may produce the same output at a lower cost, increasing profits. Even before profits rise, optimism around AI could lift valuations. In a bear scenario, fears around AI or overinvestment could result in asset price declines. For consumers: If corporate profits or valuations rise, consumers with equity exposure (either directly or through retirement accounts) will experience increases in wealth. records.text: We expect China’s crude imports to stay low if prices remain high because the two drivers—lower crude demand and crude draws—look largely sustainable in coming quarters. Few Meaningful Practical Examples One of the best-known examples of bundling municipal infrastructure in Germany is the school PPP project implemented by the district of Offenbach. By combining approximately 90 school buildings, a project volume was created in the early 2000s that proved a ttractive to private investors. The schools themselves were not sold, but their refurbishment, financing and operation were transferred to private partners under long -term contracts. Once these contracts expired, however, the district reassumed full respon sibility for the schools. The example therefore illustrates both the potential of bundling municipal infrastructure and the limits of permanently involving private capital in core public functions. The rarity of such projects reflects the generally limited political acceptance of these arrangements. In many cases, municipalities would need to cooperate closely and reach political compromises in order to create projects of sufficient scale. Such cooperation can fail simply because local political majorities differ. It cannot be ruled out that municipalities may, as a result of continuing financial pressure, increasingly consider selling infrastructure assets or opening operations to private strategic investors in the years ahead. records.text: Global Economic Viewpoint | 08 September 2026 47 Structurally low growth feeds fiscal risk Mexico's low-growth problem persists, and a look at GDP per capita shows that at the margin the problem may be deepening: GDP per capita has grown just 0.4% over three decades and has contracted since 2018. That, plus falling growth expectations, could accelerate fiscal deterioration, which is one of the main reasons we see Mexico on a path to losing investment grade over the next two to three years unless it starts growing much more or does a significant fiscal consolidation (see report Mexico Watch). But we do not expect a significant consolidation anytime soon, we expect a fiscal deficit of 4- 5% of GDP this year and next. Weak growth may also explain softening consumption as households adjust to lower expected permanent income. Inflation near target, but it will likely rebound Headline inflation hit 3.1% yoy in July, very close to Banxico’s 3% target, although core held at 4.0% on sticky services. We expect headline to rebound as agricultural prices mean-revert, in fact the rebound has already started with headline at 3.3% yoy in the first half of August, and with some impact from El Niño. Remember that in Mexico oil pass-through stays limited as gasoline prices are controlled. Core should hold near 4%, as services ease slowly following weak economic activity, but goods face upside risk from a potentially weaker MXN. The banks themselves are not shrinking their committed capital to the BDCs, which is a signal of support for the private credit market (Figure 5). Effectively banks are still happy to collect extra fees on these committed capital lines, allowing borrowing bases to do much of the credit quality control for them, while not signalling much concern over a broader increase in default risk that would increase capital charges on these committed lines. And the key sector risk for this entire market is software, where non-accrual rates are still limited (Figure 8), and where rating agency downgrades are also effectively non-existent, despite the rapid YTD widening in software spreads (Figure 9). But our conclusion to be structurally negative on the space continues. High PIK rates and sharply wider software leveraged loan spreads portend higher non- accrual rates & downgrade rates ahead, which will test private credit funds in future quarters. And for many smaller BDCs & interval funds that are not depicted here, fund flow pressures could prove problematic, with bank revolvers a primary source of liquidity given little access to $IG bond markets. IT (+142%), Insurers n (+140%), Materials (+78% yoy), Energy (+52%), Brokers (+58%) and Pharma (+20%) were among the strongest contributors. records.text: 8 September 2026 Focus Germany Deutsche Bank AG Page 9 Private companies can be extensively involved in various construction and operating models. Under build -operate-transfer models, or BOT models, the private partner finances, plans, builds and operates an infrastructure asset for a specified period. At the end of this period, which corresponds to the term of the concession, the infrastructure is transferred back to the public sector. Under build-own-operate models, or BOO models, private-sector involvement goes one step further. Following the construction phase, the private company retains ownership of the infrastructure for an indefinite period. There is no obligation to transfer the infrastructure back to the public sector. Such models allow responsibilities to be allocated very individually between the public and private sectors. Private companies can therefore be involved at an earlier stage and to a greater extent. One example is a design -build-finance- operate-maintain concession. This is a comprehensive project model under which a private company is responsible for all phases of a project, from planning to long- term maintenance. This method is often used for large infrastructure projects with a long service life. Such models are generally financed through user charges or fixed payments from the public sector. Some would argue that it is still too early to see second-round effects, and we would expect the MPC minutes at this meeting to make the same point, hedging against risks that evidence builds. However, even then, there is no sign of them in forward-looking measures such as the DMP wage expectations, which were a central plank of the MPC's monitoring framework laid out in July. Measures that have picked up (notably the Citi/YouGov measure of household inflation expectations) remain lower than previous peaks and have shown themselves able to reverse quickly when and if geopolitics allows, and so we think it would take a more prolonged period of elevation for these series to move the central MPC members, although we expect them to acknowledge the risks at this meeting. Other data flow has been broadly in line with MPC expectation There has been little news in other data that would, in our view, move any of the MPC members from their prior positions. Unemployment as measured by the LFS remains noisy, while non-LFS measures of employment point to a stagnant picture, consistent with the MPC's assessment in July. The reported improvements in some survey measures (KPMG/REC) only move from contraction to flat, while the DMP , PMI and our own shadow employment indicator using Revelio data show no signs of growth. records.text: Michael Metcalfe, Caroline Coughlin 07 Sept 2026 US inflation: Marginal consensus risks When short-term rates markets are this balanced, fine margins matter more than they should. August CPI may be a case in point. While all expect a solid, energy -driven rise in headline CPI, a handful of basis points in State Street PriceStats’ granular data suggest the market may now be too complacent about core inflation after recent downside misses. Headline inflation is relatively straightforward. The State Street PriceStats index rose 0.4% in August on a non -seasonally adjusted basis, the largest monthly increase since May, after two months of flat or falling prices (Figure 1). Although smaller than the initial energy-driven jumps after the Iran conflict began, the rise is enough to partly reverse the recent decline in annual PriceStats inflation (see chart here). Energy and transportation prices again drove much of the increase, rising nearly 1.4% on the month (Figure 2). If this disruption to disinflation were confined to energy, as it largely has been so far, it might not be too problematic. But this month, the danger is likely in the detail. The State Street PriceStats sector series show food, health and beauty price increases broadly in line with seasonal norms. Apparel, electronics and, to a lesser extent, household equipment recorded above -average rises (Figure 2). records.text: Modest Price Upgrade Despite Assumption Shipping Disruptions Continue The price upgrade is modest despite our new assumption that shipping disruptions continue because OECD commercial oil inventories have so far barely drawn since the war began, and because we assume Mideast supply adaptation continues. Reason 1: Resilient OECD Commercial Stocks OECD commercial land inventories—a key predictor of crude prices—have barely drawn so far since the war began (Exhibit 3), leaving our end-August OECD commercial oil stocks counter 119mb above our July balance estimate. The limited OECD commercial draw reflects a smaller-than-expected deficit amid market adaptation, and an unusually large concentration of global draws in OECD SPR, on water, and in China. Deficit narrows. We estimate that the global oil market deficit has narrowed from about 7mb/d in March 2026 to 1mb/d in 2026Q3, as Gulf output partially recovered on higher pipeline use and dark flows, Asia demand remained weak, and ex Gulf output grew (Exhibit 4). Our 2026Q3 1mb/d deficit is 5.4mb/d smaller than the 6.4mb/d Q3 drop in Persian Gulf output vs. its 2025 average, reflecting a 1) 1.2mb/d surplus in 2025, 2) 2.7mb/d weaker demand (vs. 2025), and 3) 1.4mb/d stronger ex Gulf production (vs. 2025). Since then, UKA prices have increasingly traded as a proxy for such a linkage. Although progress has slowed due to the change of prime minister in the UK and the postponement of the July 2026 EU–UK summit, we think the linkage thesis remains intact. Key preparatory work has already been completed, signalling steady policy convergence. The UK’s scheduled removal of the Carbon Price Support in April 2028 will eliminate a key asymmetry between carbon pricing in the UK and EU power sectors. Both systems have also moved toward broader maritime coverage, while the European Partnership Bill announced in May could provide a legislative route to fast-track future UK–EU agreements. We see strong incentives for both sides to reconvene following the parliamentary summer recess. With no new summit date confirmed at the time of writing, we see late 2026 as a plausible window for a political agreement or roadmap. Risks remain: Despite our positive outlook, several risks remain. The EU ETS reform proposals include a slower LRF, a lower MSR absorption rate and extended free allocation for energy-intensive industries (see page 10). Angola: Fiscal disappoints, growth and inflation surprise positively Fiscal performance is on course to underperform the budget targets (and investor expectations) despite the elevated level of oil prices. If the authorities manage to bring the primary balance close to breakeven in H2, we expect the deficit for FY2026 to reach 3.9% of GDP, barely down from 4.0% in 2025 (see Angola Viewpoint 27 August 2026). records.text: Ben Luk 7 September 2026 1 Insights Information Classification: General “Key Charts to Watch” for China (Q 4 26) CNY Quiet Safe Haven. Despite persistent geopolitical tensions, rising inflation expectations, repeated currency interventions and periodic commodity shocks, China has emerged as a relative safe haven. The CNY has quietly appreciated by 3.8% against the USD year-to-date, making it Asia’s second best-performing currency, while the RMB CFETS basket has also gained 3.9% against China’s trading partners. Although a weaker dollar has supported EM currencies broadly, the PBoC has successfully engineered a stronger CNY through a steady fixing bias, while implied FX volatility has fallen to a multi -year low (Figure 1). We expect USDCNY to retain a gradual downward bias, with our PriceStats PPP model indicating a long-term fair value of 6.33—around 5.8% below current levels (Figure 2). However, Beijing is unlikely to tolerate such rapid appreciation, particularly as 2026 is already the CNY’s fourth-best year of the past 15 years. Real money investors nevertheless continue to extend their CNY overweight, with holdings remaining in the top quintile over the past three months, reflecting the currency’s perceived safe -haven role within EM (Figure 3). Recent FX flows and media sentiment also remain supportive (Figure 4). Overall, we expect the PBoC to permit a controlled appreciation of both the CNY against the USD and the CFETS basket, supported by Beijing’s reduced emphasis

Searching science for new power Advancing existing technologies but also undertaking fundamental scientific research into potentially entirely new breakthrough technologies are also crucial. The former includes ongoing efficiency improvements in solar and batteries, advanced drilling technologies (eg, for deeper geothermal sources), innovation in nuclear reactor designs and alternative fissile materials (eg, thorium instead of uranium). The biggest game changer could be a breakthrough in commercially viable nuclear fusion power. It could solve the 'trilemma' of security, sustainability, and cost, which could radically alter the geo-economics of energy. However, as we wrote in Fusion: Tomorrow's solution to today's problem, our base case is that cost-competitive, grid-scale fusion power only emerges in the 2040s. It is thus unlikely to be a panacea for the near-term power demand challenge. For technological advancements, especially for such scientific challenges as turning commercial fusion into reality, scientific capabilities and access to capital for the necessary large long-term investments will be crucial. records.text: 8 September 2026 Focus Germany Deutsche Bank AG Page 25 Remuneration Models for Renewable Energy Become More Diverse From an investor’s perspective, it is important that revenue models for renewable energy installations are becoming increasingly diversified. EEG -based remuneration schemes will remain relevant for smaller PV installations for the time being. At the same t ime, direct marketing and power purchase agreements (PPAs) are gaining importance. Direct marketing is already mandatory above certain plant-size thresholds. This is generally implemented through the market premium model. Under this system, the operator no longer sells electricity at a fixed feed -in tariff to the grid operator but instead markets it through a direct marketer on the electricity exchange. In addition, the operator receives a market premium that compensates for the difference between the suppo rt level assigned to the installation and the market value of the electricity produced. Economically, this creates a revenue stream broadly aligned with EEG support levels while integrating the installation into market-based electricity system logic and creating incentives for market-oriented and system-supportive behaviour. If the market value exceeds the reference support level, no market premium is paid; if it falls below that level, the premium compensates for the difference. The growing presence of nonbank lenders in FHA and Ginnie Mae programs is a central concern for liquidity risk and counterparty strength. Nonbanks now represent over 90% of Ginnie Mae servicing, a large reversal from 2008 when banks held roughly 60%. To address structural liquidity challenges, Ginnie Mae implemented additional loan-level functionality within its securities that would increase the tradability and value of Ginnie Mae mortgage servicing rights. The agency is also exploring new acknowledgment agreement structures with warehouse lenders to give nonbank issuers broader access to capital. Nonbank lenders now originate ~77% of all US residential mortgages, and that concentration is a growing source of liquidity and counterparty risk. Key question: does the upside inflation risk from the energy supply/demand imbalance overwhelm other disinflationary forces? This creates a tension in the market narrative. For several months/quarters now, the inflation discourse has gravitated toward the idea that AI is near-term inflationary but medium-term disinflationary (for instance, see A Claudy inflation outlook for our thinking on the topic back in March, and Inflation has a memory problem, where we explore one facet of AI-related inflation). But what if this is wrong, or at a minimum, overly simplistic? While we still strongly sympathize with that framework on a basic level, a more nuanced take would need to acknowledge that the path to any eventual productivity dividend may itself be energy and commodity intensive. The focus of this note is therefore on a growing upside risk that may be underappreciated in inflation pricing: energy. Their revenue is increasingly being driven by the other effects of the re flation trade: fee revenue. records.text: 7 September 2026 Germany Blog Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG AfD wins elections, but falls short of an absolute majority to form a government Yesterday's election results were remarkable in many aspects. First, the far-right AfD fared even better than in the latest polls, winning 43.8% of total votes according to preliminary official results (see here). Second, tactical voting led to almost all smaller parties being represented in the new parliament. Third, the result of the Conservatives looks crushing at first sight (minus 19 pp), but one has to take into account that they lost some votes to the Greens and SPD due to tactical voting (redistribution in the centrist party camp). Fourth, voter turnout was very high, reaching 77.8% (vs. 60.3% in 2021). In the new six-party regional parliament neither the AfD (39 out of 83 seats) nor the centrist parties combined with the tacit support of the Left (39) have an absolute or even relative majority to elect a state premier. This leaves us with a complex post- election set-up. Thus, the populist BSW, with its 5 seats, has a key role to play in the upcoming coalition negotiations as potential kingmakers. While the AfD missed their 45+% / absolute majority election target, they missed it so narrowly that it seems difficult for them to not aim for governing Saxony-Anhalt. records.text: Assessing Sensitivity of EM European Equities to Natural Gas Shocks European natural gas inventories remain at relatively low levels, while the outlook for LNG supply availability is still uncertain, amid still subdued Persian Gulf export volumes owing to the US-Iran war. The re-escalation of the conflict since early July has pushed up TTF prices by 70% to above 70 EUR/Mwh. While our commodities team’s base-case forecast for 4Q26 TTF stands at EUR 53/MWh, they acknowledge that if Middle East energy exports do not normalize, Dec26 TTF prices would likely need to rise above EUR 100/MWh to materially curb LNG demand from Asia in order to meet storage requirements ahead of the winter season. Against this backdrop, we examine the sensitivity of EM equities — particularly in EMEA markets — to identify the markets and sectors that are likely to be most exposed to gas price shocks, using two approaches. First, we model the historical sensitivity of EM equity returns to changes in natural gas prices, while controlling for key macro variables including growth, FX, rates, and global equities. Compared with other EM markets, EM European markets—particularly CEE and Greece—show the highest negative sensitivity to higher gas prices, based on one-month-forward TTF. He emphasized the Fed’s commitment to returning PCE inflation to 2%, focusing on underlying trends rather than isolated data points, and argued that softer summer inflation readings do not signal meaningful improvement in underlying inflation. In our view, these comments raised the bar for the Fed to remain on hold in September (see report: US Watch: Warsh hikes the credibility trail at Jackson Hole). Warsh’s remarks also appeared to acknowledge residual seasonality in both inflation and employment data, which tend to weaken later in the year (Exhibit 6). The way to deal with this issue is to smooth through 12 months of data, since residual seasonality is a zero-sum game over a full year. And 12-month inflation gauges are problematic across the board, albeit to different degrees. Additionally, nominal GDP and consumer spending growth are trending above 5% (Exhibit 7). That simply isn’t consistent with 2% inflation unless the Fed believes the real economy can grow faster than 3%. It doesn’t. That is, there is a very real risk that the futures curves are underpricing upside risk. More broadly, a persistent energy deficit would have implications beyond the direct contribution of energy prices to headline inflation. One of the defining features of the post-GFC period was abundant and relatively inexpensive energy, which encouraged investors and policymakers to treat energy shocks as largely transitory. An AI-driven increase in energy demand could challenge that assumption. If markets begin to view energy scarcity as a multi- year structural phenomenon, rather than a cyclical fluctuation, the result may be a higher inflation risk premium embedded in nominal yields, inflation swaps, and breakevens. There is also a convexity dynamic to watch in the inflation indices via the weight in the basket. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 5 Introduction: Tracking AI's trail through the US economy AI investment has been booming with few signs of slowing in 2026. Not only have hyperscalers repeatedly raised their capital expenditure plans, with greater shares of this spending financed through equity and debt offerings, but token usage by the rest of the business sector has gradually moved higher, pointing to greater usage and penetration. AI infrastructure investment so far appears relatively insensitive to the business cycle, geopolitical risks, and even interest rates, at least among firms with stronger credit quality. Understanding the outlook for the US economy requires a thorough understanding of AI spending and how it permeates the National Income and Product Accounts. To better understand AI and its effects and account for the evolution of the AI investment cycle, we have revisited our approach. In particular, we refine our framework to account for AI's contribution to GDP growth along three dimensions. First, we include more investment categories and improve our treatment of imports, which increases the accuracy of our estimates. Second, we now compute AI's contribution to growth in two ways: a broad approach and a narrow approach. The broad approach captures spending that could be used for AI, whether or not it actually is, while the narrow approach attempts to estimate the portion of that spending actually attributable to the AI boom. Lower-income, less-educated consumers are at less risk of displacement, but face more near-term price pressures and stand to benefit less from AI- related job and wealth creation. Net Effects: CHIC households benefit most in the base case as wealth effects and task creation offset labor displacement The next question is how these exposures will balance out. As described above, our base case is that AI will raise productivity, and positive effects from wage growth, task creation, and wealth effects will offset the rise in unemployment. In this scenario, we expect CHIC households to benefit most. Some high-income, highly-educated workers may face temporary periods of softer consumption, especially younger workers that likely have greater risk of displacement and lower accumulated equity wealth. That said, for this group's spending as a whole, substantial levels of equity wealth relative to labor income mean that relatively modest gains in asset prices can offset the spending effects of declines in labor income. In our base case, CHIC households are best off, reaping the largest gains from financial asset appreciation and also from eventual wage gains and disinflation.

Private transport companies also provide operating services on individual local public transport routes on behalf of the public sector. PPPs additionally exist for public administrative buildings and schools. Despite these examples, public -private partnerships are frequently viewed critically in political debate in Germany and often receive little political support. One common concern is whether private companies can actually provide the specified services at a lower cost than the public sector, given that private companies seek to earn a return and face higher financing costs than the state. However, such assessments often overlook the fact that politically desired projects involving private participation and partial private financing can frequently be implemented more quickly than projects without such participation. Biogas and synthetic fuels: Political support is increasing again Following the 2025 federal election, the political assessment of bioenergy has improved fundamentally. This applies both to biogas in the heating market and to biofuels in the transport sector. In the heating sector, biogas is increasingly regarded as a complementary and system-supportive element of the heating transition. Under the Building Modernization Act, biogas and biomethane are recognized as compliance options for renewable heating requirements. At the same time, political priorities do not focus on broad-based volume expansion but rather on those applications in which bioenergy can exploit its specific advantages. These include combined heat and power generation and the injection of biomethane into existing gas infrastructure. This could provide existing facilities with a long-term investment perspective and allow them to align their operating patterns more closely with system requirements. Many aspects of social infrastructure are also co-financed by state budgets. The states provide grants to municipalities and independent providers, for example for constructing and operating childcare centers, youth centers, sports facilities and libraries. The states are also responsible for disaster management and generally provide grants for equipping fire services. Counties, cities and municipalities The importance of cities and municipalities, as well as counties as associations of municipalities, in providing public infrastructure is often underestimated. Take n together, however, Germany’s more than 10,000 cities and municipalities, spread across almost 300 counties and supplemented by more than 100 independent cities, account for a considerable share of public fixed investment. records.text: M Idea 2 The Signals Through the Noise Year-to-date, the major US stock indices are up double digits, already putting them on track for another strong year of returns. In fact, this is one of the broadest year of returns in recent memory, with the S&P 500, Dow Industrials, Nasdaq 100, Nasdaq Composite all up between 13-16%, and the Russell 2000 up 20%. This is in contrast to the past few years, when returns were narrower and more concentrated in large cap AI-related stocks, especially the enablers (a.k.a the picks and shovels). In line with our outlook for this year, market performance has broadened driven by earnings growth. EPS growth for the median stock in the Russell 3000 is currently running in the mid-teens, which is driving a much broader return profile in the US stock market (Exhibit 1 ). This has all coincided with what we have deemed a new economic cycle that began at the trough of the rolling recession around Liberation Day in April 2025. The reacceleration in sales growth has led to a v-shaped rebound in EPS growth as operating leverage returned to the median company. This was a classic early-cycle dynamic that has supported our primary thesis over the past year, which remains out of consensus—i.e., a new economic and earnings cycle began in April of last year. Morgan Strategic Research The age profile of today’s homebuyer looks very different from that of previous generations. According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), the median age of first-time buyers has climbed to a record 40, up from the late 20s in the 1980s, as high rents and student loan debt make saving for a down payment difficult. Repeat buyers are older, with a median age of 62, and the typical home seller is now 64, the highest ever recorded. Baby Boomers (ages 60–78) have emerged as the largest share of both buyers and sellers, and their wealth accumulation has made them more active in housing transactions relative to younger generations. The traditional family household is also becoming less representative of who is buying homes. Just 24% of recent buyers have children under the age of 18, down from 58% in 1985. Rising childcare costs have also limited families’ ability to save for a down payment. The housing market is increasingly becoming shaped by older, often single buyers, while younger cohorts, Millennials and Gen Z, continue to face high barriers to entry. Investment and expenditure in water services frequently account for a large share of municipal investment plans and budgets. The renovation or replacement of drinking-water p ipelines and sewers is generally particularly expensive. An investment backlog often develops in this area because some forms of damage to networks are not immediately detected. From a financial perspective, investment in water infrastructure is therefore a sleeping giant. Drinking-water supply and wastewater disposal are frequently operated by municipally owned enterprises, special -purpose associations or municipal utilities. In some cases, particularly in larger cities, these responsibilities are transferred to private companies. These companies operate waterworks, elevated reservoirs, pumping stations, wastewater treatment plants and the associated networks. Most costs are financed by users through fees, such as water and wastewater charges, and, in some cases, through initial connection charges for water and wastewater services. Waste management also falls within the remit of municipalities. Counties are generally responsible for organizing waste disposal, including collection, transport, recycling and recovery, and landfill disposal. BDC fund outflows, stale software loan valuations, a rising share of PIK loans, and some evidence that bank revolvers are shrinking due to underlying portfolio deterioration are all worsening headwinds. Given that most private credit and software debt is borrowed at floating-rates, the prospect of multiple Fed hikes through 2027 will only exacerbate these problems. For now, the tactical pressure on BDCs is muted . Easier financial conditions elsewhere are allowing large BDCs to obtain liquidity from $IG corporate bond and securitized markets, while software defaults remain muted. In addition, rating agency assessments are widely diverging from market prices, with spec-grade software downgrades at a minimum despite a massive YTD widening in credit spreads. But as we move forward in time, a relatively simple cocktail of continued AI adoption + a Lev Loan software maturity wall that needs to start being refinanced in Q1'27 + Fed hikes would put more considerable pressure on BDC liquidity and fundamentals. Japan’s Physical AI: Current status and future outlook What we learned • The term “Physical AI” is often used broadly, but the concept itself is not new. It generally refers to AI systems that operate in the physical world, where the output is motion rather than text. What is genuinely new, however, is the emergence of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. These models enable robotic systems to perceive, reason, and act autonomously without explicit pre-programming. Humanoid robots represent just one possible form factor for deploying these capabilities in the physical world. • The key bottlenecks limiting broader adoption of Physical AI robotics today are system integration, data availability, and the development of advanced hands and grippers. Given current technological constraints, achieving a VLA model with capabilities comparable to ChatGPT remains a long-term challenge. As a result, greater efforts are needed to consolidate the vast amount of robotics-related data into unified datasets that can be used for development. The shortage of high-quality data is also slowing progress in the development of robotic hands and grippers. • Japan has a clear advantage in robotics hardware manufacturing, controllers, and the deployment of automation systems. Our impression was that investor interest in the food and beverage sector has increased somewhat compared with previous years. However, investors were highly selective rather than broadly positive on the sector, focusing on the visibility of profit growth and valuations of individual stocks. By subsector, condiments attracted relatively strong interest due to their high sales growth, while investor interest in beer, soft drinks and instant noodles was relatively limited given their challenging earnings outlooks. In the near term, some investors were concerned that higher costs related to the Middle East situation could slow earnings momentum from the next quarter into the second half. An El Niño event is defined when the ONI exceeds +0.5°C for five consecutive overlapping three‑month periods. The strength of the event is determined by the magnitude of the anomaly: +0.5°C is considered weak, +1.0°C moderate, +1.5°C strong, and +2.0°C very strong. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 9 assumes a "representative household". It therefore does not capture the behaviors and outcomes of different cohorts of consumers. Consumer subgroups differ in the types of work they do, their levels of income and wealth, their responses to changes in the economic backdrop, and the goods and services they purchase. As a result, the effects of AI will not be uniform. In this note, we focus on differential effects across four demographic factors: income, education, region, and age. In each section, we show as much detail as the data allow, but we cannot break down every channel of exposure across all demographic subgroups. That said, we find some common threads: the exposures and potential outcomes for college-educated, high- income, city-dwelling consumers, which we refer to as "CHIC" households, tend to be similar. Meanwhile, the effects for low-income, non-college-educated, and rural consumers tend to be similar. This makes sense given the overlap among these groups. CHIC households tend to work white-collar jobs, are more sensitive to asset market moves, and spend relatively more on discretionary services and big-ticket items. Meanwhile, the opposite is true for the second group; these households are more dependent on labor market income and spend relatively more on essentials (Exhibit 7 ). Further distinction comes when we include age. Within our CHIC group, we expect different outcomes for older, more experienced workers versus younge

records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 35 Appendix: Tracking Cohort-Level Data Our base case is only one possible path, so we will track cohort-level data for evidence that outcomes are evolving differently. In this section, we show the cohort-level data we will be tracking on a monthly and quarterly basis to glean how the outlook for different consumer cohorts is changing. We also highlight two quarterly trackers we are producing related to AI and the economy: 1) our AI labor tracker, which tracks employment and unemployment rate across AI occupation groups, and 2) our AI productivity tracker, which tracks productivity growth across AI industry groups. Labor Market We highlight two measures of wage growth by income cohort. The first is our own calculation ( Exhibit 53 ). For this, we group detailed industries into low-, middle-, and high- income cohorts based on that industry's average earnings from 2019. We then track growth in average hourly earnings across those groups over time. The second is the Atlanta Fed's measure (Exhibit 54 ). Their measure is built from the household survey, rather than the establishment survey, and tracks the same consumers over time. They then compute each consumer's YoY wage growth and take a 12m moving average of the medians. records.text: 7 September 2026 UK economic notes Deutsche Bank AG Page 2 Services: small contraction into the summer There will be a number of offsetting forces impacting the services economy. The hot dry weather will have certainly buoyed activity a touch. Alongside the World Cup, we expect some consumer facing services output to have benefitted from better weather. Business services, however, we think could see some contraction. Taken together, we expect the services sector to have shrunk by 0.1% m-o-m. What industries lifted activity? For starters, longer trading hours on World Cup match days will have boosted hospitality output. Indeed, the latest RSM/CGA Hospitality Tracker showed a 1.4% y-o-y lift in July. This marked the strongest month of the year so far and the third-best result in the Tracker since the start of 2025. We also expect transport and storage output to have risen by 0.4% m -o-m with our models continuing to point to upward momentum. Our forecast is broadly in line with Bloomberg consensus, which currently stands at 0.2% m/m for core CPI. It is slightly above CPI fixings, which at the time of writing imply headline inflation of 3.39% y/y. From a rounding perspective, a core CPI print of 0.3% is more likely than 0.1%. The main upside risk is a larger rebound in nonhousing core services than we expect, particularly in lodging away from home and household operations. Goods inflation could also prove firmer if the increase in electronics prices persists because of bi-monthly CPI sampling. records.text: European Economics 07 September 2026 Citi Research 2 Unpacking the Remarkable Endurance During the first half of 2026, European growth defied expectations. Economic data have consistently outperformed, pushing the Citi Economic Surprise Index to record-high territory (see Fig 1). This endurance, remarkable in the face of still- elevated energy prices and growing competition of Chinese products, has been driven by two key macro pillars, in our view: A. Stockpiling – An export recovery took hold since the spring related, we think, to a global stockpiling cycle amid tight supply conditions and fears of future price hikes. Both exports and industrial activity have picked up since the spring (see Fig 2). Exports towards Asia and Eastern Europe, the two important suppliers into the European industrial sector, indeed drove the pickup in foreign sales. We note this has become a recurrent dynamic in recent years: more frequent supply disruptions tend to trigger large inventory-building cycles – it happened after Covid, after US tariff announcements and now Strait of Hormuz closures – blurring the demand signal. When demand should in principle slow down as confidence tanks, in fact production is ratcheted up to build buffers. However, stockpiling-driven growth is by definition short-lived. Figure 1. records.text: 14 Global Economic Viewpoint | 08 September 2026 The main reason for the revision is that the coordinated FX intervention has raised the stakes around Japan's defense of the yen. However, the intervention is not the sole reason for the revision. Even before the intervention, the BoJ had acknowledged the risk of underlying inflation overshooting 2%, and support within the Policy Board for faster rate hikes had begun to broaden. The focus of monetary policy has gradually shifted from lifting underlying inflation toward 2% to preventing it from exceeding 2%. Whether the next hike comes in September or October, we expect the next three hikes to be delivered at a much faster pace than in 2024-25. Beyond 1.75%, however, the path becomes more uncertain. Our base case assumes USD/JPY falls to 149 by end-2026 and 145 by end-2027, allowing the BoJ to reach 2% in July 2027. If the yen instead remains around 155 or above, we think the BoJ may need to raise rates to 2.5%. Conversely, a global risk-off shock that strengthens the yen and weakens demand could end the cycle at 1.5%-1.75%. records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 11 From AI-related spending to AI-only spending One challenge in estimating the effects of AI on activity is that the starting point may be too broad. To some degree, this was by necessity. Splitting investment into its AI and non- AI components is difficult since the National Income and Product Accounts (NIPA) accounts report investment by asset class – spending on equipment, intellectual property products, and structures – rather than by end use. Our prior published estimates began with four categories that we believe contain large amounts of AI spending, including information processing equipment in equipment spending, software in intellectual property products, and data centers and power centers in structures investment. These categories are where AI investment likely shows up, but reflect investment regardless of whether the underlying activities are AI-related. Hence, even with a more refined accounting for imports, we still begin the process of estimating the contribution of AI investment to GDP growth with spending categories that include both AI and non-AI spending. We call this "AI-related" spending since we know it comes from both AI and non-AI sources, with the understanding that the acceleration in spending in these components likely reflects the AI boom. records.text: 8 September 2026 Focus Germany Deutsche Bank AG Page 35 For institutional investors, fiber-optic networks are generally attractive when projects can be bundled into sufficiently large clusters or portfolios. The key consideration is not merely network deployment but also network utilization, that is, the actual take -up rate. Fiber networks become more attractive investment opportunities when a high share of connected, or potentially connected customers sign contracts and generate recurring revenues. This represents an important difference from the energy sector. Whereas revenues from electricity networks are largely secured through regulation, the commercial success of fiber-optic networks depends much more heavily on customer acquisition, competitive dynamics and utilization rates. Overall, fiber-optic infrastructure is better described as a scalable platform investment than as a typical stand -alone project. Strategic investors, including telecommunications companies and regional network operators, undertake deployment, operation and marketing. In stitutional investors can participate through equity investments, infrastructure platforms, bonds or debt financing. This is already evident in several major German fiber platforms. This should help re-anchor growth in 2028, when we expect it to climb back to 1.7%. Risks to the outlook While changes to our global outlook have been modest, it remains key to consider the risks to the view. In this regard, we continue to flag the same risks, but in a somewhat different order. The global economy will have to digest tighter financial conditions We have long pointed to stubborn inflation in the US triggering Fed hikes as a key risk to the outlook. It appears this risk is becoming reality. However, to the extent that Fed hikes coincide with still solid US growth, worst case scenarios should be avoided. Nevertheless, in a context where loose financial conditions and AI have been driving stock markets and fueling consumption via wealth effects, the risk of a tightening of financial conditions may still be the Achilles’ heel of the global economy. Fed hikes, potentially coupled with a correction in global equity prices, could feedback via negative wealth effects, triggering a contraction. records.text: Japan Research | 08 September 2026 11 CFR’s Rush Doshi: US-China relationship: Technology, trade, defense and its impact on Asia Xiangjin Lyu BofAS Japan kerwin.lyu@bofa.com Rush Doshi, C.V. Starr Senior Fellow for Asia Studies and Director of the China Strategy Initiative at the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), presented a talk entitled “US-China relationship: Technology, trade, defense and its Impact on Asia.” Chris Oberoi, our Head of APAC Equity Research, served as moderator. The main takeaways from the talk are as follows. Technology is shifting the balance of warfare toward defense Rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI), drones, swarms, and autonomous systems are driving the most significant changes in warfare in decades, increasing range, precision, and lethality while giving defenders an asymmetric advantage. The Russia- Ukraine war has demonstrated how the extensive use of drones can enable deep strikes far beyond the front line and constrain territorial advances. Iran has also shown that even with degraded conventional forces, a country can threaten freedom of navigation through relatively low-cost missiles. Shifting trade patterns are raising deindustrialization risks The traditional globalization model, which was shaped by surplus economies exporting to the US market running a large trade deficit, faces growing pressure as the US increasingly attaches conditions to market access through tariff policies. records.text: Net Upside Price Risks and Recommendations Risks to our price forecast remain significantly tilted to the upside on net, especially near-term. Key upside price risks include more intense and geographically broader shipping disruptions, and damage to crude production or export Infrastructure, which could weaken output in the Mideast or elsewhere for longer. We see the risk of larger or more persistent supply disruptions as especially high in and around Hormuz, the Red Sea and the Black Sea (Exhibit 14). The main downside price risks are a faster Mideast output recovery and stickier demand losses. Our base case assumes 0.7mb/d of demand scarring in 2027, or 12% of the 6mb/d 2026Q2 loss versus a no war scenario. We illustrate the significant net upside price risks with two Gulf output and Brent scenarios (Exhibit 15): Price upside scenario: Brent might exceed $120/bbl if 2027 average Gulf output n remains 4mb/d below pre-war levels, versus 0.5mb/d below in our base case. We view more intense shipping attacks in Hormuz and the Red Sea as the most likely driver of this lower-output, higher-price scenario. Price downside scenario: Brent might decline into the $60s in 2027 if 2027 average n Gulf output rises 1mb/d above pre-war levels. We still recommend hedging geopolitical risk through deferred Mar27-Dec27 European diesel timespreads, which would rise over 100% if persistent Russia or Mideast refinery outages keep the nearby 9-month spread near current levels. records.text: 2 Asia Viewpoint | 08 September 2026 Asia back-to-school outlook Growth divergence & tightening bias remain unchanged The macro picture in Asia hasn’t changed much compared to that in June when we published our mid-year outlook (see note, Mid-Year review: Stronger growth on AI tailwinds, but divergence deepens). Just like three months ago, geopolitical uncertainty remains elevated, but robust global demand for tech goods still offers support to resilient regional growth. Thanks to strong 2Q26 performance in some economies, we are pushing up Asia growth forecast to 4.8% in 2026 (from 4.7% previously). That said, we revise down our 2027 Asia growth forecast to 4.5% primarily on weaker growth momentum in China. On the back of the growth forecast upgrade, we expect cross-country divergence to continue between tech exporters vs non-exporters, amid lingering risks on inflation and shocks from potential Fed hikes. As still, we maintain our view that regional central banks will hold on to their tightening bias in 2H2026. External demand to stay as growth driver through 2028 Tech capex continues to drive Asia exports higher Despite persistent geopolitical uncertainty and weaker domestic demand from China, growth resilience remains in the region, supported by stronger-than-expected external demand. This expectation rests on three key points: • In the July MPR assessment, the MPC reconfirmed the principles guiding the QT programme. These were: that Bank Rate is the active tool of monetary; that sales do not disrupt the functioning of financial markets, and only in appropriate market conditions; and that sales are predictable and gradual. The first means that QT should not be adjusted in response to the macro environment (unless Bank Rate is constrained, which it is not). records.text: M Foundation 8 Setting the Stage: Our Framework and Assumptions Grounding in our Prior Work: Our Base Case for AI For this analysis, we build off the results of our prior work on AI and Economic Transition. In our recent note, we used a general-equilibrium framework to assess potential labor market outcomes of AI. In doing so, we found the amount of AI disruption is largely dependent on three forces: 1) the speed of AI adoption, 2) the speed and quantity of new task creation, and 3) indirect feedback loops such as wealth effects. These results are intuitive. Slower diffusion gives workers more time to adapt, faster task creation creates new employment opportunities, and stronger asset markets support demand, and in turn, labor demand. As a result, assuming faster diffusion or excluding offsets from task creation and wealth effects leads to much more extreme conclusions. In our "base case", we assume a moderate speed of diffusion, which is still 2x that of the Internet (e.g. AI diffuses in about a decade versus two previously). We link the pace of task creation to the speed of diffusion and assume wealth effects that are smaller than those observed historically, to be conservative. In this scenario, the outcome is relatively optimistic; AI boosts productivity without triggering a downturn. While both seek to benefit from the planned expansion of infrastructure, their moti vations, investment criteria and degree of operational involvement differ considerably. This distinction is important for understanding the channels and instruments through which private capital can be mobilized for infrastructure investment. Institutional investors include pension funds, investment management companies, hedge funds, insurance companies and sovereign wealth funds. They act primarily as providers of capital. Their focus lies on generating stable, long - term and inflation -protected returns while preserving and increasing the long - term value of their assets. Institutional investors typically favor passive investments with limited operational complexity, whereby capital is channeled into infrastructure through funds, bonds or direct project participations.
