records.text: M Foundation Morgan Stanley Research 3 Executive Summary Key takeaway: In our base case outlook for AI adoption and economic transition, AI boosts productivity without a large rise in unemployment, as task creation and wealth effects are offsets to labor market disruption. In this outcome, we expect AI to disproportionately benefit college-educated, high-income, city-dwelling ("CHIC") households over the longer run, a contrary view to the conventional wisdom that white-collar households are the most AI-vulnerable cohort. This is based on our findings across three key channels: Labor markets: CHIC workers have high occupational exposure to AI. This brings risk but also opportunity; these workers are exposed to displacement, but also to productivity gains and new jobs. Wealth: CHIC households, and particularly older CHIC households, have greater equity exposure, resulting in larger spending impacts for these households from AI- driven gains in capital returns. Inflation: CHIC households are more exposed to longer run AI-driven disinflation in services and less exposed to potential near term AI-related inflation pressures. Importantly, among CHIC households, outcomes likely vary by career stage. Established, older professionals may be well positioned to capture AI-related productivity and asset-price gains. Highly-educated younger professionals may be more vulnerable, as AI may substitute for entry-level tasks with less offset from wealth. These distinctions matter for macroecon

Translating AI spending into growth is difficult since capex does not translate one-for- one into US GDP. Corporate capex measures what firms spend on long-term assets. GDP, on the other hand, measures final output of domestically produced goods and services. Spending on intermediate goods is therefore not counted, while spending on imported final goods and services is subtracted. In the case of AI investment, spending on imported equipment used in data center construction is included in corporate capex plans but does not contribute to US GDP. First, we improve the accuracy of our import offset. We adjust imports for re-exports, so that only imported goods that remain in the US are netted out of spending. Second, we estimate the share of those imports purchased by businesses for private fixed investment, as imports can also be purchased by consumers or governments. Third, we expand the adjustment beyond imports of computers and peripherals to also include semiconductors and related devices. Although the supply of chips and memory, and the associated inflationary pressures, have been widely discussed this year, semiconductor imports were previously much smaller and slower-growing than imports of computers and peripherals. records.text: Weekly data through 28 Aug 2026. We construct four components: 1) risk reversals, 2) MSCI France/MSCI Europe ratio, 3) 10y OAT-Bund spreads, and 4) FX positioning. In the first step of the process, we construct the components for risk reversals and FX positioning. For risk reversals we use an equally weighted average of the full-sample z-scores applied to EUR-USD and EUR-CHF risk reversals, 3 months and 1 year ahead. For FX positioning we use a simple average of the z-scores for the CFTC data (non-commercials, TFF Asset Managers, and TFF Leveraged Funds) and SDR FX options. In the second step of the process, we generate full-sample z-scores for all four components separately (re-standardising onto a common scale) and then take their simple average. In the third step of the process, we calculate the full-sample z-score of that average, which becomes our proxy for France-related risks. Throughout, the signs of individual components have been adjusted so that higher z-scores suggest higher France- related concerns. Our approach is inspired by Lina Fransson and Oskar Tysklind (2017), An index for financial conditions in Sweden, Sveriges Riksbank Economic Review 2017:1. In the data so far, our work on AI and labor market disruption finds that AI is causing some excess unemployment in occupations with high AI exposure (typically white collar professions with computer-facing tasks), but effects remain relatively small. In this note, we extend the analysis to refine our base and bear case outcomes by including outlooks for consumers across four demographic factors: income, education, region, and age. While our prior work provides a baseline for the economy and monitors the incoming data against this view, it does not speak directly to differential effects across consumers. Using micro data on occupations, consumer balance sheets, and spending patterns, we examine exposures of each cohort across the three transmission channels, which in turn helps us develop base and bear case expectations for each. Incomplete projects continue to weaken trust in the pre-sale model, keeping households reluctant to buy new homes even when mortgage costs fall or purchase rules ease. A genuine reset would require larger and better-coordinated support that directly addresses inventory, incomplete projects and developer balance sheets. The policy toolkit includes a national stability fund, central-government-led destocking, stronger project-completion guarantees, public and affordable housing expansion, broader removal of purchase restrictions, housing provident fund support, mortgage subsidies, inventory purchases, land exchanges and a clearer framework for developer liabilities. Urban renewal can support construction demand, improve older housing quality, activate idle assets and connect resale-market liquidity with upgrade demand, but it cannot by itself resolve the national inventory overhang or unfinished-project risk. A convincing reset would require three conditions: sustained improvement in volumes, prices and inventories beyond tier-1 cities; credible completion of unfinished projects and restored confidence in new homes; and nationally coordinated destocking and balance-sheet repair rather than repeated local easing. To be clear, that doesn’t mean prices normalise; but in our view it does mean they should come off as winter progresses. See Tight, risky – but not panicky, dated 24 August, for more details. Obviously, the sooner Middle Eastern LNG returns, the earlier gas prices will peak. In the immediate resolution scenario, we therefore assume prices would dip sharply to about EUR30–35/MWh in Q1 2027. The slope down until then is determined by the speed of the supply recovery. We assume LNG flows can normalise within about two months; we also believe the ramp-up will be front loaded in the first month as the northern (undamaged) trains appear to be able to hit the ground running. Of course, without Middle Eastern LNG, this winter looks quite dire. In its absence, the combination of low storage levels at the start of winter and significant ongoing draws would result in gas storage in Europe potentially dropping below 10% ( see Figure 4). That would imply TTF rises well into the triple-digit range as prices will have to curtail demand at its most inelastic point of the year. The BoJ is playing catchup In Japan, we highlight our recent revisions to the BoJ path, primarily but not solely driven by the coordinated FX intervention to support the yen. Our new base case is for the BoJ to accelerate to a roughly quarterly pace, with hikes in September and December 2026 and March and July 2027, taking the policy rate to 2%. However, the terminal rate could be sensitive to the exchange rate and global factors. The coordinated FX intervention has raised the stakes around Japan's defense of the yen, calling for a change in fundamentals, as otherwise a BoJ behind the curve would likely undermine the effectiveness of such intervention. records.text: 2 Global Economic Viewpoint | 08 September 2026 Global letter: Surfing the supply shocks Claudio Irigoyen BofAS Antonio Gabriel BofAS Surfing the supply shocks The global economy has continued to prove resilient despite the energy shock and the Iran war, on the back of the AI-driven investment boom in the US and the export cycle in Asia. As we have long been arguing, the global economy has become less sensitive to oil prices over time. But risks will continue to build as long as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains low and the need to rebuild oil inventories eventually surfaces. Resiliency amid the turbulence remains the base case, but there are relevant risks on the horizon beyond the energy shock. With Fed hikes imminent as soon as September and the demand for capital to finance the AI investment boom in the US boosting long-term interest rates at the margin, the world will have to cope with tighter financial conditions. Our core views remain broadly unchanged: the US remains on solid footing, and persistently high inflation will drive Fed hikes starting this month; China’s domestic demand weakness will remain amid policy complacency; and Europe’s insufficient demand will eventually drive the ECB depo rate to or below 2% next year. Policy continuity in focus We note that Serbia’s extremely appealing macro case is largely based on robust policy framework with prudent and tight fiscal policy as well as transparent monetary framework with credible Serbian Dinar (RSD) peg. Therefore, rising risks of a potential change also increases risks of a material revision of policy framework. We admit that even in case of political change, the policy will likely remain robust and aligned with IMF Policy Coordination Instrument (PCI) parameters as well as European Union (EU) accession process. However, the overall policy sustainability after elections is yet to be reaffirmed. Approaching elections have already triggered revision of the country’s budget with some 0.5% of GDP in additional social spending. The bulk of the spending boost (coming as planned social transfers) is due already this month, which is likely to help to support real GDP growth in late 2026 and likely pushing it closer to our 3.5% target. However, the size of the additional spending appears to be fairly modest, so we do not view this move as a potential risk to the overall fiscal outlook. Investment Grade (IG) within reach Passage of electoral cycle has important implications for Serbia sovereign rating. records.text: ill-tight supply/demand conditions should largely drive rental outcomes in the short term, with the quarterly vacancy rate to hold around current levels (0.7%q/q - 0.8%q/q) this year and next. Ending negative gearing could raise rents by requiring investors to restore after‑tax yields. However, this assumes landlords had prior ability to raise rents but have chosen not to. It also overlooks market‑clearing conditions, such as vacancy rates which empirically are strongly correlated with rental growth. Our Australia economists view grandfathering of the policy (existing arrangements are not affected) materially blunts any near‑term effect on rents. Existing investors retain their current tax treatment, avoiding a sudden repricing of the rental stock, limiting the scope for new post‑budget investors to push through above‑market rent increases. Various theories have been put forward to explain this pattern, but none have fully described the problem. It now appears we have the reverse. By some metrics, UK productivity growth is finally on the rise. Building on our productivity analysis from earlier this year, we show evidence it is primarily driven by ICT, although other sectors that benefit from AI advancements also play a role. We think this development is both positive and meaningful, although we remain cautious. The UK is experiencing a new productivity puzzle — After 15 years of sluggish productivity growth (let’s call it the “OG” productivity puzzle), the opposite is finally happening, although the causes of this boost to productivity are not yet fully clear. We think this is a meaningful shift, but it is sensitive to the data used — The improvement is best seen when using HMRC’s RTI (PAYE) data. Annual productivity growth averaged 1.2% per quarter since 2024Q3. The white-collar sector is leading the way, and ICT is the flag bearer — Since 2025, ICT contributed over a third of the annual productivity (PAYE) growth, despite comprising less than 10% of the entire economy. records.text: 14 Japan Research | 08 September 2026 JGB yields could peak slightly above 3% Rising JGB yields reflect two main factors. First, as monetary policy normalizes, banks have less need to hold JGBs and greater incentives to lend to the real economy. Second, investors are demanding higher risk premiums amid uncertainty over Japan’s monetary and fiscal policies. At current higher yields, JGBs are increasingly being viewed as attractive investable assets. Meanwhile, a faster pace of BoJ rate hikes could reduce the monetary policy risk premium by lowering uncertainty around the policy path. As a result, the 10-year JGB yield is likely to peak only slightly above 3%. Improving fundamentals support a more constructive yen outlook The outlook for the yen has become more constructive as Japan’s fundamentals improve. The current account surplus has widened to around 5% of GDP, while inward foreign direct investment (FD)I has increased. Structural outflows arising from digital-services payments and NISA investment are being offset by stronger semiconductor-related trade flows and foreign inflows into Japanese equities. Recent yen weakness may reflect FX hedging associated with the strong performance of Japanese equities rather than a deterioration in Japan’s fundamentals. Coordinated FX intervention and expectations of faster BoJ rate hikes should provide additional support, underpinning our revised year-end USD/JPY forecast of 149. records.text: European Economics 07 September 2026 Citi Research 6 Inflation Outlook Higher gas prices inevitably lift the headline inflation profile, with the gas-to-HICP passthrough taking longer than oil. The inflation “hump” now looks taller and longer than previously estimated, peaking at 3.7%–3.8% YY by year-end (see Fig 9), on our forecasts. But more fundamentally, we believe the resilience of the economy discussed above speaks to marginally more inflationary pressure than in our initial expectation. The inflation self-correcting mechanism (higher inflation => lower demand => lower inflation) weakens if exogenous shocks trigger higher output (to build buffers) rather than lower demand. The higher inflation peak in 4Q26E may also influence spring 2027 wage negotiations, potentially preventing wage growth to ease further (as we currently still expect). That said, we still view the risk of a wage-price spiral developing from here as very limited. The overall softness in hiring and labor market momentum reduces workers' collective bargaining power, especially compared to the last gas price shock in 2022. And soft private consumption limits firms’ pricing power (as evidenced in firms’ lower selling prices in August, despite the rally in energy prices). Six months since the Iran conflict started, we think signs of second-round effects remain muted.
